# SECTION D — Backend Development Fundamentals (30 Questions)

**1. What is the difference between frontend and backend development?**
Frontend is everything the user sees and interacts with directly — buttons, forms, layout. Backend is the part that runs on the server, handling data, logic and security behind the scenes. The frontend talks to the backend through APIs.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION D — Backend Development Fundamentals (30 Questions)

text:
**2. What is an API?**
A set of rules that allows two programs to communicate. A frontend app calls an API to request data from a backend, and the backend responds with the requested information.

**3. What is the difference between a GET and a POST request?**
GET retrieves data from the server without changing anything — like loading a webpage. POST sends new data to the server, such as submitting a form or creating a new record.

**4. What is a database and why is it needed?**
A database stores data permanently so it can be retrieved later, even after the server restarts. Without one, all information — user accounts, orders — would disappear immediately.

**5. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?**
Authentication checks **who you are**, usually through a username and password. Authorization checks **what you are allowed to do** once you are logged in, such as whether you can access admin features.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 4. What is a database and why is it needed?

text:
**6. What is a status code, and what does 404 mean?**
A number the server sends back to indicate the result of a request. 404 means "Not Found" — the requested resource does not exist. 200 means success and 500 means a server error occurred.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 6. What is a status code, and what does 404 mean?

text:
**7. What is caching and why does it improve performance?**
Caching stores frequently requested data temporarily so it can be returned quickly without recalculating or re-fetching it every time. This reduces load on the database and makes responses much faster.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 7. What is caching and why does it improve performance?

text:
**8. What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?**
SQL databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) store data in structured tables with fixed relationships. NoSQL databases (MongoDB) store data in flexible formats, useful when the structure of data changes often.

**9. What is middleware in a backend application?**
Code that runs between receiving a request and sending a response. It is commonly used for checking authentication, logging requests, or validating input before the main logic runs.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 8. What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?

text:
**10. What is the request-response cycle?**
The full process of a client sending a request to a server and receiving a response back. The client sends a request, the server processes it (often involving a database), and then sends a response with the result.

**11. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous programming?**
Synchronous code runs one task at a time, waiting for each to finish before starting the next. Asynchronous code can start a task and move on to other work while waiting — useful for slow operations like network calls.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 11. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous programming?

text:
**12. What is a token, and why is it used instead of a password for every request?**
A token is a piece of data generated after a successful login that proves a user is authenticated. Instead of sending a password with every request, the client sends the token, which is faster and safer.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 12. What is a token, and why is it used instead of a password for every request?

text:
**13. What does it mean for a backend system to be "scalable"?**
A scalable system continues to perform well as the number of users or amount of data grows. This is achieved through techniques like caching, load balancing and efficient database design.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 13. What does it mean for a backend system to be "scalable"?

text:
**14. What is a server, in simple terms?**
A computer that is always running and listening for requests. When a client sends a request, the server processes it and sends back a response — like a waiter taking and delivering orders in a restaurant.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 14. What is a server, in simple terms?

text:
**15. What is REST, and why is it commonly used for APIs?**
REST is a set of conventions for designing APIs using standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. It is widely used because it is simple, predictable and works well over the web.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 15. What is REST, and why is it commonly used for APIs?

text:
**16. What is SQL injection, and why is it dangerous?**
An attack where a malicious user inserts harmful SQL code into an input field to manipulate or steal data from a database. It is dangerous because it can expose or destroy sensitive information. **Always use parameterized queries to prevent it.**

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 16. What is SQL injection, and why is it dangerous?

text:
**17. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH requests?**
PUT replaces an entire resource with new data. PATCH updates only specific fields, leaving the rest unchanged. PATCH is more efficient when only small changes are needed.

**18. Why is error handling important in backend development?**
Good error handling prevents the application from crashing and gives clear, useful feedback when something goes wrong — such as returning a helpful message instead of a confusing technical error.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 17. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH requests?

text:
**19. What is the role of environment variables in a backend project?**
They store configuration values like database passwords or API keys **outside the actual code**. This keeps sensitive information secure and makes it easy to use different settings for development and production.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 19. What is the role of environment variables in a backend project?

text:
**20. What is the difference between a monolith and microservices?**
A monolith is a single application containing all features in one codebase. Microservices break the application into many small, independent services, each handling one specific feature, which can be deployed and scaled separately.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 20. What is the difference between a monolith and microservices?

text:
**21. What is load balancing, and why is it used?**
Load balancing distributes incoming requests across multiple servers so no single server becomes overwhelmed. It improves reliability and keeps the application fast even with many users.

**22. What is the most important skill for a backend developer to have?**
Clear logical thinking and the ability to break a big problem into small, manageable steps. Tools and languages can be learned over time, but methodical reasoning is the foundation.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 21. What is load balancing, and why is it used?

text:
**23. What is database indexing?**
An index is a special data structure that makes searching a database table much faster, similar to an index at the back of a book. Without one, the database must check every row to find a match.

**24. Why should passwords never be stored as plain text?**
If a database is ever compromised, plain text passwords are immediately exposed and reusable by attackers. Passwords are hashed using a one-way function so even if the data leaks, the originals cannot be recovered.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 24. Why should passwords never be stored as plain text?

text:
**25. What is rate limiting and why is it useful?**
Rate limiting restricts how many requests a user or system can make within a certain time period. It protects the backend from abuse, prevents overload, and reduces the risk of certain attacks.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 25. What is rate limiting and why is it useful?

text:
**26. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?**
Vertical scaling means making a single server more powerful by adding memory or processing power. Horizontal scaling means adding more servers to share the load, working together as a group.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 26. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

text:
**27. What is JSON, and why is it commonly used in APIs?**
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight format for structuring data using key-value pairs. It is widely used because it is easy for both humans to read and machines to parse.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 27. What is JSON, and why is it commonly used in APIs?

text:
**28. What happens if a backend server goes down?**
Users cannot access the application or receive an error response. Well-designed systems use multiple servers and load balancers so that if one fails, others continue handling traffic without the application going fully offline.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 28. What happens if a backend server goes down?

text:
**29. What is the purpose of logging in a backend application?**
Logging records what happens inside an application over time — requests received, errors that occurred, actions taken. It is essential for debugging problems and understanding system behaviour in production.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 29. What is the purpose of logging in a backend application?

text:
**30. Why is it important to validate user input on the backend, not just the frontend?**
Frontend validation can be bypassed by a user calling the API directly. Backend validation is the final, trusted checkpoint that ensures no invalid or harmful data is processed or stored, regardless of how the request was made.

> **Closing thought:** backend development is built on a small set of core ideas — servers, APIs, databases, authentication and communication — repeated and combined in different ways. Master these fundamentals deeply, explain them simply, and you are well prepared.

# SECTION E — Multithreading & Concurrency Scenarios (70)

These are scenario-style questions. For each one, state the problem, name the tool, and explain the trade-off. Detailed code for the key patterns is in Part 17 of the notes.

## E1–E10: Basics, synchronization, async aggregation

**1. Thread lifecycle in action.** Explain all six states (New, Runnable, Running, Blocked, Waiting, Terminated) and what moves a thread between them.

**2. Runnable vs Thread in a web application.** Which do you choose and why? *Answer:* `Runnable`, because Java only allows single inheritance, so extending `Thread` uses up your one `extends`. It also separates the task from the thread that runs it, which is what executors and lambdas need. Future scope: switch to `Callable` for return values, use `ExecutorService` to manage threads at scale, and with virtual threads (Loom) `Runnable` becomes even more important for lightweight concurrency.

text: **3. Synchronization for a shared resource.** In an online ticket booking system, two users update the seat count at the same time and cause overbooking. *Answer:* a classic race condition — use a `synchronized` method so only one thread modifies the shared resource at a time. For counters, `AtomicInteger` is lighter. For read-heavy cases use `ReadWriteLock`. In distributed systems combine with database-level locking or optimistic concurrency.

Exclusive DB update without collisions.** Two threads update the same customer row. *Answer:* guard the critical section with a `ReentrantLock`, use `tryLock` with a timeout to avoid indefinite blocking, and always unlock in `finally`. **8. Gracefully shutting down an ExecutorService.** *Answer:* `shutdown()` -> `awaitTermination()` -> if needed `shutdownNow()` -> await again. Restore the interrupt status when catching `InterruptedException`, and log the dropped queue for visibility.

**9. Dependent asynchronous tasks.** Task B (dispatch) must only run if Task A (payment) succeeds. *Answer:* `thenCompose`. `thenCombine` is for two *independent* tasks whose results you merge. This avoids nested blocking `Future.get()` calls.

# SECTION F — System Design

## F1 — The seven-step answer template

Use this structure for **every** system design question.

1. **Clarify requirements** — functional (core features, users, interaction channels, data types, integrations) and non-functional (read-heavy or write-heavy, availability, latency, consistency, rate limiting)
2. **Capacity estimation** — daily/monthly users, peak concurrency, read/write RPS, storage, cache memory, bandwidth
3. **High-level design** — clients, application servers, load balancers, services, databases, storage, caching, message queues, external services
4. **Database design** — data modelling, entities and relationships, choosing the right storage, schema and access patterns
5. **API design** — which endpoints to expose, which style (REST, GraphQL, RPC), which protocols (HTTPS, WebSockets, gRPC, AMQP/MQTT)
6. **Dive deep into key components** — whatever the interviewer focuses on (short-URL generation, real-time message delivery, sharding, replication, cache invalidation)
7. **Address key concerns** — scalability and performance (scale up/out, caching, indexing, denormalization, sharding, async), and reliability (identify single points of failure, redundancy, geographic redundancy, replication, circuit breakers, retries with exponential backoff, monitoring and alerting)

## F2 — The ten most common questions

**1. Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL).**
*Functional:* generate a unique short URL; redirect to the original; optional custom short URLs; link expiration; optional usage analytics.
*Non-functional:* 99.9% availability; millisecond latency for shortening and redirects; millions of requests per day; durability for years; security against phishing.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: F2 — The ten most common questions

text:
**2. Design a Chat Application (WhatsApp).**
*Functional:* one-on-one and group conversations; online/offline status; delivery statuses (sent, delivered, read); multimedia messages; push notifications.
*Non-functional:* real-time delivery with minimal latency; millions of concurrent users; high availability (may be compromised in favour of consistency); durability — messages must not be lost.

**3. Design a Social Media Platform (Instagram).**
*Functional:* upload and share images and videos; like, comment and share; follow and unfollow; generate a news feed; tagging in posts and comments.
*Non-functional:* 99.9% availability; low latency for feed generation; millions of concurrent users; high durability for uploads; eventual consistency is acceptable.

**4. Design a Video Streaming Service (YouTube).**
*Functional:* upload videos with titles, descriptions, tags and thumbnails; on-demand streaming; search for videos, channels and playlists; like, dislike, comment and share; record view counts.
*Non-functional:* 99.99% uptime; real-time, lag-free streaming; horizontal scalability; high durability.

**5. Design an E-commerce Platform (Amazon).**
*Functional:* sellers list products with details; cart and wishlist; search by product, category and brand; place orders for one or many products; rate and review purchased products.
*Non-functional:* millions of users, products and transactions simultaneously; 99.9% availability; low latency for page loads, search and checkout; high durability for user data, listings and orders.

**6. Design a Ride-Sharing Service (Uber).**
*Functional:* see nearby available drivers; book a ride with pickup and drop-off; real-time matching; real-time cost and ETA estimation from distance, traffic and demand; real-time tracking for rider and driver.
*Non-functional:* millions of users and rides; low latency for matching, GPS tracking and requests; 99.9% uptime; a consistent view of the system for riders and drivers.

**7. Design a File Storage Service (Google Drive).**
*Functional:* upload files of various types and sizes; download on demand; share files and folders via links or email invitations; search by name, type, content or metadata; synchronize across devices.
*Non-functional:* millions of users and billions of files; low-latency uploads, downloads and search; high availability; consistency across devices during sync; durability.

metadata.title: JAVA-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 7. Design a File Storage Service (Google Drive).

text:
**8. Design a Web Crawler.**
*Functional:* fetch URLs efficiently; handle different content types (text, images, multimedia); prioritise URLs by criteria such as importance and freshness; store crawled data efficiently.
*Non-functional:* scale to millions or billions of pages; minimal fetch and processing latency; maximise pages crawled per unit of time.

**9. Design a Notification System.**
*Functional:* support email, SMS, push (mobile/web) and in-app channels; support transactional, promotional and informational types; schedule notifications; send in bulk for campaigns; automatically retry failed deliveries.
*Non-functional:* millions of notifications per minute at peak; 99.99% uptime; low latency for real-time and high-priority notifications; reliable delivery across all channels.

**10. Design a Logging and Monitoring System.**
*Functional:* collect logs from applications, servers, databases and microservices; support multiple formats (JSON, plaintext, XML); archive old logs to cold storage; powerful querying by time range, log level, source and other attributes; alerts on patterns, thresholds or anomalies.
*Non-functional:* horizontal scalability for growing log volume; low-latency ingestion and processing for real-time monitoring; 99.99% uptime; durability with replication across nodes or data centres.

1.3 Client–server architecture
Almost every application you use follows the client–server model. The client (a browser, mobile
app, or another server) sends a request. The server — the backend application you'll build in this
course — receives it, does work, and sends back a response.
Key properties of this model:
The client never touches the database directly — it always goes through the server
One server can handle requests from thousands of different clients
The server enforces rules the client can't be trusted to enforce (e.g. "only the account owner
can withdraw money")

An API (Application Programming Interface) is the contract that lets the client and server talk. It
defines: what URLs exist, what data to send, and what data comes back. Later in this course you
will build REST APIs — the dominant style of API for web and mobile backends — using Spring Boot.

always sit in front of a database like PostgreSQL or MySQL.

3.1 History and features
Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, built around the promise "write once, run

javac compiles human-readable source into bytecode — a platform-neutral instruction set. The

Chapter 9 — Inheritance
Inheritance lets a class (subclass) reuse and extend another class's (superclass) fields and
methods — an IS-A relationship: a Dog IS-A Animal.
public class Animal {
protected String name;
public Animal(String name) { this.name = name; }
public void makeSound() { System.out.println(name + " makes a sound"); }
}
public class Dog extends Animal {
public Dog(String name) {
super(name);

// calls Animal's constructor first

}
@Override
public void makeSound() {

// overriding — replaces parent behavior

System.out.println(name + " barks");
}
}

Constructor chaining: every subclass constructor implicitly (or explicitly via super(...)) calls a
superclass constructor first, so the object is fully initialized top-down.
+

+
THINK LIKE A DEVELOPER — COMPOSITION VS. INHERITANCE

Inheritance is powerful but rigid: it locks a subclass to one parent's implementation forever.
"Favor composition over inheritance" means: when in doubt, give a class a reference to
another object (has-a) rather than extending it (is-a). A Car should have an Engine, not be

an Engine. Spring Beans lean almost entirely on composition via dependency injection —
Part 16 builds on this directly.

Strings
A String in Java is immutable — once created, its contents never change. Every "modifying"
operation returns a brand-new String.
String s = "hello";
s.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s);

// returns "HELLO" — does NOT change s
// still "hello"

s = s.toUpperCase();

// now s refers to the new object

String literals live in the string pool, a special memory region that reuses identical literals:
String a = "test";
String b = "test";
System.out.println(a == b);

// true — same pooled object

String c = new String("test");
System.out.println(a == c);

// false — c is a distinct heap object

System.out.println(a.equals(c));

// true — same content

Because Strings are immutable, repeated concatenation in a loop creates many throwaway
objects — use StringBuilder (not thread-safe, fast) or StringBuffer (thread-safe,
slower) instead.

for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
sb.append(i).append(",");

// mutates the same buffer — O(1) amortized per append

}

HOW HASHMAP WORKS INTERNALLY

A HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets. hashCode() on the key picks a bucket;
entries in the same bucket (a hash collision) form a linked list, or — since Java 8 — a redblack tree once a bucket exceeds 8 entries, keeping worst-case lookup O(log n) instead of
O(n). Overriding equals() without also overriding hashCode() (or vice versa) breaks
HashMap/HashSet — always override both together.

RECRUITER PER SPECTIVE

"Which List/Map implementation would you use here, and why?" is one of the most common
Java screening questions. The correct habit isn't memorizing Big-O — it's naming the actual
access pattern (random reads? frequent inserts at the front? need sorted order? need
thread safety?) and picking the structure that matches it.

Generics
Generics let a class or method operate on a type specified by the caller, catching type errors at
compile time instead of runtime.
public class Box<T> {

// generic class

private T content;
public void set(T content) { this.content = content; }
public T get() { return content; }
}
Box<String> box = new Box<>();
box.set("hello");
// box.set(42);

// compile error — caught early, not at runtime

public static <T> T firstElement(List<T> list) {

// generic method

return list.get(0);
}

Bounded types restrict what T can be; wildcards handle "unknown but related" types, governed by
the mnemonic PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super:
<T extends Number> double sum(List<T> nums) { ... }

// bounded — T must be a Number

void copy(List<? extends Number> source, List<? super Number> dest) {
// source PRODUCES values you read (extends) —
// dest CONSUMES values you write (super)
}

Type erasure: generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks types, then erases them,
compiling Box<String> and Box<Integer> down to the same bytecode using Object internally
with inserted casts. This is why you can't do new T() or check instanceof T at runtime.

Class loading
Classes are loaded lazily, on first use, in three phases: Loading (reading the .class file into
memory), Linking (verifying bytecode, allocating memory for static fields, resolving references),
and Initialization (running static initializers and static field assignments). A hierarchy of class
loaders (Bootstrap → Platform → Application) delegates upward first, so core Java classes can
never be shadowed by application code.

The heap is further divided generationally: Young Generation (Eden + two Survivor spaces, where
new objects are born and most die quickly) and Old Generation (long-lived objects promoted after
surviving several collections). This generational split exists because most objects die young —
collecting Young Gen frequently and cheaply is far more efficient than scanning the whole heap
every time.

JIT compilation
The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode (slow but instant startup). The JIT (Just-In-Time)
compiler monitors which methods run frequently ("hot" methods) and compiles them directly to
native machine code at runtime, so repeated execution gets much faster — this is why longrunning Java processes often perform better the longer they run ("warm-up").

Concept

Meaning

Normalization
Form

Rule

1NF

Every column holds a single, atomic value — no repeating groups or lists in a cell

2NF

1NF + every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not part of it

3NF

Normalization eliminates data duplication and update anomalies, at the cost of needing joins to
reassemble related data. Real systems sometimes deliberately denormalize (duplicate some data)
to optimize read-heavy paths — a tradeoff, not a rule violation.

Durability

Once committed, data survives even a crash immediately after

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

-- both updates succeed together, or neither does

Indexes
An index is a separate, sorted data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows by
a column's value without scanning the whole table — trading extra storage and slower writes for
much faster reads on that column.

(WHERE/ORDER BY). Don't over-index — every extra index slows down every INSERT/UPDATE

The DAO pattern
public interface EmployeeDao {

List<Employee> findAll();

public class JdbcEmployeeDao implements EmployeeDao {
private final DataSource dataSource;
public JdbcEmployeeDao(DataSource dataSource) { this.dataSource = dataSource; }
public Optional<Employee> findById(int id) {
String sql = "SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE id = ?";
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
PreparedStatement stmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
stmt.setInt(1, id);
try (ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery()) {
return rs.next()
? Optional.of(new Employee(rs.getInt("id"), rs.getString("name")))
: Optional.empty();
}
} catch (SQLException e) {
throw new RuntimeException("Query failed", e);
}
}
// findAll(), save() follow the same shape
}

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {
@ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleNotFound(ProductNotFoundException ex) {
return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
.body(new ErrorResponse("NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage()));
}
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException
ex) {
String message = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
.map(f -> f.getField() + ": " + f.getDefaultMessage())
.collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(new ErrorResponse("VALIDATION_ERROR",
message));
}
}
public record ErrorResponse(String code, String message) {}

One centralized @RestControllerAdvice catches exceptions thrown anywhere in the controller
layer and converts them into consistent JSON error responses — no repeated try/catch in
every endpoint.

Returning your JPA @Entity directly from a controller leaks database structure into the

public class JwtService {
private final SecretKey key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secretBytes);
public String generateToken(String username, List<String> roles) {
return Jwts.builder()
.subject(username)
.claim("roles", roles)
.issuedAt(new Date())
.expiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + 900_000))

// 15 min

.signWith(key)
.compact();
}
public String extractUsername(String token) {
return Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build()
.parseSignedClaims(token).getPayload().getSubject();
}
}
public class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
FilterChain chain) {
String header = req.getHeader("Authorization");
if (header != null && header.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
String token = header.substring(7);
String username = jwtService.extractUsername(token);
if (username != null && jwtService.isValid(token)) {
var auth = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(username, null,
authorities);
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
}
}
chain.doFilter(req, res);
}
}

PART 25 · REDIS & CACHING

Part 25 — Redis & Caching
Caching strategies · TTL & invalidation · Spring Cache · Redis integration · Distributed caching

Why cache
A cache stores the result of an expensive operation (a slow query, a computed report) in fast
storage, so repeated requests skip the expensive path. Redis is an in-memory key-value store
commonly used as a cache layer in front of a relational database.

Cache-aside pattern
read(id):
value = cache.get(id)
if value == null:
value = database.get(id)

// cache miss — go to the source of truth

cache.put(id, value, ttl)
return value
write(id, value):
database.save(id, value)
cache.evict(id)

// invalidate — don't leave stale data cached

This is the cache-aside (lazy-loading) pattern: the application checks the cache first, falls back to
the database on a miss, and populates the cache for next time. On write, the safest default is to
evict the cache entry rather than try to update it in place.

<!-- page 107 -->
Spring Cache abstraction
@EnableCaching
@Configuration
public class CacheConfig {}
@Service
public class ProductService {
@Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id")
public ProductResponse getById(Long id) {
return productRepository.findById(id).map(this::toResponse).orElseThrow();
}
@CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id")
public void update(Long id, ProductRequest request) { ... }
@CachePut(value = "products", key = "#result.id()")
public ProductResponse create(ProductRequest request) { ... }
}

@Cacheable checks the cache before running the method, and stores the result if it wasn't
already there. @CacheEvict removes an entry (used on update/delete). @CachePut always runs
the method and refreshes the cache with the result.

Wiring Redis

data:
redis:
host: localhost
port: 6379
cache:
type: redis

time-to-live: 600000

# 10 minutes, in ms

TTL (time-to-live) automatically expires an entry after a set duration — the simplest, most robust
invalidation strategy for data that's allowed to be briefly stale (product listings, dashboards) rather
than data that must always be perfectly fresh (an account balance).

PRO TIP

In a multi-instance deployment, an in-memory (per-JVM) cache gives every instance a
different, inconsistent view. Redis's shared, external cache means every application
instance sees the same cached value — essential once you run more than one replica.

Part 26 — Docker

Images vs. containers
An image is a read-only, versioned snapshot of everything an application needs (code, runtime,
libraries, OS layers). A container is a running instance of an image — isolated from the host and
other containers, but sharing the host's kernel (lighter than a full virtual machine).

Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app
# Multi-stage build — keeps the final image small
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src

# cache dependencies in their own layer

RUN mvn package -DskipTests
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

+

+
PRO TIP

A multi-stage build uses one stage with the full Maven+JDK toolchain to compile, then
copies only the resulting jar into a slim JRE-only final image — the shipped image doesn't
carry Maven, source code, or build tools, cutting its size dramatically.

(every read sees the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a response, possibly stale).
You cannot have all three simultaneously during a partition — most real systems pick a practical
point between "strong" and "eventual" consistency based on the use case (a bank balance leans
consistent; a social media like-count leans available).

Core Java & OOP
Q: Why is Java considered platform-independent, and what actually crosses platforms?
A: Source compiles to bytecode (not native machine code); any machine with a matching JVM can
run that same bytecode. The JVM is platform-specific, but the bytecode it consumes is not.
Q: Why does Java pass everything "by value," even objects?
A: A reference variable holds a value — the memory address of an object. Passing it to a method
copies that address, not the object. The method can mutate the object through the copied
reference, but reassigning the parameter itself never affects the caller's variable.
Q: Why can't static methods be overridden?
A: Static methods are resolved at compile time based on the reference type (static/early binding),
not the runtime object type — this is "method hiding," not overriding, and dynamic dispatch never
enters the picture.
Q: equals() vs. hashCode() — what's the contract?
A: Equal objects (per equals()) must produce the same hashCode(); unequal objects may or may
not. Breaking this contract corrupts hash-based collections like HashMap/HashSet.

Collections & Generics
Q: Why does ArrayList resizing cost O(n) occasionally but still average O(1) amortized for add()?
A: Most adds just place an element in existing capacity — O(1). When capacity is exhausted,
ArrayList allocates a new, larger array (typically 1.5×) and copies everything — O(n), but this
happens rarely enough that the average cost per add, across many adds, is still O(1).
Q: Why does modifying a List while iterating with a for-each loop throw
ConcurrentModificationException?
A: The enhanced for-loop uses an Iterator internally, which tracks a modification count.
Structurally changing the list outside the iterator's own remove() invalidates that count, and the
next next() call detects the mismatch and fails fast — better than silent, undefined behavior.
Q: What is type erasure's practical downside?

<!-- page 128 -->
A: You cannot create a generic array (new T[10]), use instanceof against a parameterized type,
or overload methods that only differ by generic type parameter — the compiler has already erased
that information by the time these checks would run.

Q: Why is a double-checked locking singleton subtle to get right?
A: Without the field being volatile, another thread can observe a partially-constructed object
due to instruction reordering — the reference can appear non-null before the constructor has
finished running.

Q: Why is ConcurrentHashMap faster than a synchronized HashMap under contention?
A: A synchronized HashMap locks the entire map for every operation. ConcurrentHashMap
partitions its internal structure so different threads can operate on different segments/buckets
concurrently without blocking each other.

Java 8+ & Streams
Q: Why can a stream only be consumed once?
A: A stream isn't a data structure — it's a one-time pipeline of operations over a source. Once a
terminal operation runs, the pipeline is considered consumed; reusing it throws
IllegalStateException by design, encouraging you to think in terms of transformations, not stored
state.
Q: When is a parallel stream actually worth using?
A: Only for large datasets with CPU-bound, independent (no shared mutable state) per-element
work — for small collections or I/O-bound work, the overhead of splitting/merging across threads
usually outweighs any benefit.

PART 34 · SPRING BOOT INTERVIEW PREPARATION

Part 34 — Spring Boot Interview Preparation

Architecture & internals
Q: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration actually decide what to configure?
A: @EnableAutoConfiguration loads a list of candidate configuration classes, each guarded by
conditional annotations (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean,
@ConditionalOnProperty). At startup, Spring evaluates each condition against your classpath
and existing bean definitions, applying only the configurations that match — and backing off
automatically wherever you've defined your own bean of the same type.
Q: What happens, in order, when a Spring Boot application starts?
A: The JVM starts → main() calls SpringApplication.run() → the ApplicationContext is
created → component scanning discovers beans → auto-configuration applies matching
configurations → beans are instantiated and dependencies injected → @PostConstruct hooks
run → for a web app, the embedded server starts listening.
Q: How does @Transactional work internally, and why doesn't self-invocation trigger it?
A: Spring wraps the bean in a dynamic proxy at startup. An external call goes through the proxy,
which opens a transaction, delegates to the real method, then commits/rolls back based on the
outcome. A method calling another @Transactional method on this bypasses the proxy entirely
(it's a direct call, not a call through the bean reference) — so the annotation is silently ignored.

Security & persistence
Q: How does Spring Security authenticate a typical JWT-based request?
A: A custom OncePerRequestFilter runs before the request reaches your controller; it extracts
the Authorization: Bearer header, validates the token's signature and expiry, loads the user's
authorities, and populates the SecurityContext. Later, @PreAuthorize/route-based rules
check that context to allow or reject the request.
Q: How does Hibernate manage entities across their lifecycle?
A: An entity is Transient until persist()-ed, becoming Managed and tracked by the persistence
context — changes to a managed entity are auto-detected ("dirty checking") and flushed on

<!-- page 131 -->
commit. It becomes Detached once the persistence context closes (e.g. after the transaction
ends), at which point changes are no longer tracked; remove() transitions it to Removed.
Q: How do you solve the N+1 problem?
A: Detect it via SQL logging (query count scaling with row count), then fix with a JPQL fetch join,
an @EntityGraph, or a batch-size hint — replacing "1 query + N lazy queries" with a single query
that fetches everything needed upfront.

Scenario-based
Q: A production endpoint is suddenly slow only under load. How do you investigate?
A: Check metrics/dashboards for the time window (CPU, memory, DB connection pool saturation,
GC pauses). Check for an N+1 query newly introduced. Check thread dumps for blocked threads (a
lock contention or a slow downstream dependency). Check whether a circuit breaker/timeout is
missing on a call to a degraded dependency, causing thread starvation upstream.
Q: How would you design a scalable REST API for a system expecting 10x traffic growth?
A: Stateless services behind a load balancer (horizontal scaling), a cache layer for hot reads,
pagination on all list endpoints, async processing (Kafka) for non-critical-path work, database
read replicas, and connection pooling sized to the expected concurrency — validated with load
testing before the growth actually arrives.

DEBUGGING-BASED

Q: A bean fails to start with BeanCreationException: Circular reference. What's
happening and how do you fix it?
A: Two beans depend on each other via constructor injection, so neither can be fully
constructed first. Fix by breaking the cycle — typically by extracting the shared
responsibility into a third bean, or (last resort) using setter injection for one side to defer the
dependency until after construction.

Track 1 — Java
Interviewer: "Your service is throwing intermittent ConcurrentModificationExceptions. Walk
me through how you'd find and fix it."
Candidate: "That points to a collection being structurally modified while it's being iterated — likely
a shared List or Map being read in one thread while another mutates it, or a for-each loop calling
remove() directly on the collection instead of the iterator. I'd grep for iteration over that collection,
check if it's ever accessed from more than one thread, and either switch to a concurrent
collection like CopyOnWriteArrayList/ConcurrentHashMap, or use the iterator's own remove()
method and add synchronization if multiple threads are genuinely involved."
Interviewer: "Why would you choose composition over inheritance here?"
Candidate: "Inheritance locks the subclass to one parent's implementation permanently and can
violate Liskov Substitution if the subclass doesn't behave consistently with the parent's contract.
Composition — giving the class a reference to a collaborator — keeps the relationship swappable
and testable, which matters especially once the class needs to be unit tested in isolation."

Pattern: Two Pointers
// Problem: does a sorted array contain two numbers summing to target?
public boolean twoSum(int[] arr, int target) {
int left = 0, right = arr.length - 1;
while (left < right) {
int sum = arr[left] + arr[right];
if (sum == target) return true;
else if (sum < target) left++;
else right--;
}
return false;
}
// O(n) time, O(1) space — beats the brute-force O(n²) nested loop

public List<Integer> bfs(Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph, int start) {
List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
Set<Integer> visited = new HashSet<>();
Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();
queue.offer(start); visited.add(start);
while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
int node = queue.poll();
order.add(node);
for (int neighbor : graph.getOrDefault(node, List.of())) {
if (visited.add(neighbor)) queue.offer(neighbor);
}
}
return order;
}
// BFS explores level by level (shortest path in an unweighted graph);

Pattern: Dynamic Programming
// Problem: minimum coins to make amount (Coin Change)
public int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);
dp[0] = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= amount; i++) {
for (int coin : coins) {
if (coin <= i) dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1);
}
}
return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
// dp[i] = fewest coins to make amount i, built up from smaller subproblems — O(amount ×
coins)

Chapter 1. Abstract
This book contains course notes covering Enterprise Computing with Java. This comprehensive
course explores core application aspects for developing, configuring, securing, deploying, and
testing a Java-based service using a layered set of modern frameworks and libraries that can be
used to develop full services and microservices to be deployed within a container. The emphasis of
this course is on the center of the application (e.g., Spring, Spring Boot, Spring Data, and Spring
Security) and will lay the foundation for other aspects (e.g., API, SQL and NoSQL data tiers,
distributed services) covered in related courses.
Students will learn thru lecture, examples, and hands-on experience in building multi-tier
enterprise services using a configurable set of server-side technologies.
Students will learn to:
• Implement flexibly configured components and integrate them into different applications using
inversion of control, injection, and numerous configuration and auto-configuration techniques
• Implement unit and integration tests to demonstrate and verify the capabilities of their
applications using JUnit and Spock
• Implement basic API access to service logic using using modern RESTful approaches that
include JSON and XML
• Implement basic data access tiers to relational and NoSQL databases using the Spring Data
framework
• Implement security mechanisms to control access to deployed applications using the Spring
Security framework
Using modern development tools students will design and implement several significant
programming projects using the above-mentioned technologies and deploy them to an
environment that they will manage.
The course is continually updated and currently based on Java 11, Spring 5.x, and Spring Boot 2.x.

The goal of this course is to master the design and development challenges of a single application
instance to be deployed in an enterprise-ready Java application framework. This course provides
the bedrock for materializing broader architectural solutions within the body of a single instance.

This comprehensive course explores core application aspects for developing, configuring, securing,
deploying, and testing a Java-based service using a layered set of modern frameworks and libraries
that can be used to develop full services and microservices to be deployed within a container. The
emphasis of this course is on the center of the application (e.g., Spring, Spring Boot, Spring Data,
and Spring Security) and will lay the foundation for other aspects (e.g., API, SQL and NoSQL data
tiers, distributed services) covered in related courses.
Students will learn thru lecture, examples, and hands-on experience in building multi-tier
enterprise services using a configurable set of server-side technologies.

inversion of control, injection, and numerous configuration and auto-configuration techniques

Chapter 8. Code Reuse
Code reuse is the use of existing software to create new software.

[1]

We leverage code reuse to help solve either repetitive or complex tasks so that we are not repeating
ourselves, we reduce errors, and we achieve more complex goals.

8.1. Code Reuse Trade-offs
On the positive side, we do this because we have confidence that we can delegate a portion of our
job to code that has been proven to work. We should not need to again test what we are using.
On the negative side, reuse can add dependencies bringing additional size, complexity, and risk to
our solution. If all you need is a spoon — do you need to bring the entire kitchen?

8.2. Code Reuse Constructs
Code reuse can be performed using several structural techniques
Method Call
We can wrap functional logic within a method within our own code base. We can make calls to
this method from the places that require that task performed.
Classes
We can capture state and functional abstractions in a set of classes. This adds some modularity
to related reusable method calls.
Interfaces
Abstract interfaces can be defined as placeholders for things needed but supplied elsewhere.
This could be because of different options provided or details being supplied elsewhere.
Modules
Reusable constructs can be packaged into separate physical modules so that they can be flexibly
used or not used by our application.

8.3. Code Reuse Styles
There are two basic styles of code reuse and they primarily have to to with control.

Libraries are modules of reusable code that
are invoked on-demand by your code base.
Your code is in total control of the library call
flow.

Frameworks are different from callable
libraries — in that they provide some level of
control or orchestration. Your code base is
under the control of the framework. This is

Chapter 9. Frameworks
9.1. Framework Informal Description
A successful software framework is a body code that has been developed from the skeletons of
successful and unsuccessful solutions of the past and present within a common domain of
challenge. A framework is a generalization of solutions that provides for key abstractions,
opportunity for specialization, and supplies default behavior to make the on-ramp easier and also
appropriate for simpler solutions.
• "We have done this before. This is what we need and this is how we do it."
A framework is much bigger than a pattern instantiation. A pattern is commonly at the level of
specific object interactions. We typically have created or commanded something at the completion
of a pattern — but we have a long way to go in order to complete our overall solution goal.
• Pattern Completion: "that is not enough — we are not done"
• Framework Completion: "I would pay (or get paid) for that!"
A successful framework is more than many patterns grouped together. Many patterns together is
just a sea of calls — like a large city street at rush hour. There is a pattern of when people stop and
go, make turns, speed up, or yield to let someone into traffic. Individual tasks are accomplished, but
even if you could step back a bit — there is little to be understood by all the interactions.
• "Where is everyone going?"
A framework normally has a complex purpose. We have typically accomplished something of
significance or difficulty once we have harnessed a framework to perform a specific goal. Users of
frameworks are commonly not alone. Similar accomplishments are achieved by others with similar
challenges but varying requirements.

9.2. Framework Characteristics
The following distinguishing features for a framework are listed on Wikipedia.

I will use them to

structure some further explanations.
Inversion of Control (IoC)
Unlike a procedural algorithm where our concrete code makes library calls to external
components, a framework calls our code to do detailed things at certain points. All the complex
but reusable logic has been abstracted into the framework.

• "Don’t call us. We’ll call you." is a very common phrase to describe inversion of control
Default Behavior
Users of the framework do not have to supply everything. One or more selectable defaults try to
do the common, right thing.
• Remember — the framework developers have solved this before and have harvested the key
abstractions and processing from the skeletal remains of previous solutions
Extensibility
To solve the concrete case, users of the framework must be able to provide specializations that
are specific to their problem domain.
• Framework developers — understanding the problem domain — have pre-identified which
abstractions will need to be specialized by users. If they get that wrong, it is a sign of a bad
framework.
Non-modifiable Framework code
A framework has a tangible structure; well-known abstractions that perform well-defined
responsibilities. That tangible aspect is visible in each of the concrete solutions and is what
makes the product of a framework immediately understandable to other users of the
framework.
• "This is very familiar."

Chapter 11. Language Impact on
Frameworks
As stated earlier, frameworks provide a template of behavior — allowing for configuration and
specialization. Over the years, the ability to configure and to specialize has gone through significant
changes with language support.

11.1. XML Configurations
Prior to Java 5, the primary way to identify components was with an XML file. The XML file would
identify a bean class provided by the framework user. The bean class would either implement an
interface or comply with JavaBean getter/setter conventions.

11.1.1. Inheritance
Early JavaEE EJB defined a set of interfaces that represented things like stateless and stateful
sessions and persistent entity classes. End-users would implement the interface to supply
specializations for the framework. These interfaces had many callbacks that were commonly not
needed but had to be tediously implemented with noop return statements — which produced some
code bloat.

11.1.2. Java Reflection
Early Spring bean definitions used some interface implementation, but more heavily leveraged
compliance to JavaBean setter/getter behavior and Java reflection. Bean classes listed in the XML
were scanned for methods that started with "set" or "get" (or anything else specially configured)
and would form a call to them using Java reflection. This eliminated much of the need for strict
interfaces and noop boilerplate return code.

setter/getter behavior and Java reflection. Bean classes listed in the XML
were scanned for methods that started with "set" or "get" (or anything else specially configured)
and would form a call to them using Java reflection. This eliminated much of the need for strict
interfaces and noop boilerplate return code.
11.2. Annotations
By the time Java 5 and annotations arrived in 2005 (late 2004), the Java framework worlds were
drowning in XML. During that early time, everything was required to be defined. There were no
defaults.
Although changes did not seem immediate, the JavaEE frameworks like EJB 3.0/JPA 1.0 provided a
substantial example for the framework communities in 2006. They introduced "sane" defaults and a
primary (XML) and secondary (annotation) override system to give full choice and override of how
to configure. Many things just worked right out of the box and only required a minor set of
annotations to customize.
Spring went a step further and created a Java Configuration capability to be a 100% replacement
for the old XML configurations. XML files were replaced by Java classes. XML bean definitions were
replaced by annotated factory methods. Bean construction and injection was replaced by
instantiation and setter calls within the factory methods.

33

<!-- page 80 -->
Both JavaEE and Spring supported class level annotations for components that were very simple to
instantiate and followed standard injection rules.

11.3. Lambdas
Java 8 brought in lambdas and functional processing, which from a strictly syntactical viewpoint is
primarily a shorthand for writing an implementation to an interface (or abstract class) with only
one abstract method.
You will find many instances in modern libraries where a call will accept a lambda function to
implement core business functionality within the scope of the called method. Although — as
stated — this is primarily syntactical sugar, it has made method definitions so simple that many
more calls take optional lambdas to provide convenient extensions.

Chapter 12. Key Frameworks
In this section I am going to list a limited set of key Java framework highlights. In following the
primarily Java path for enterprise frameworks, you will see a remarkable change over the years.

12.1. CGI Scripts
The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) was the cornerstone web framework when Java started
coming onto the scene.

[1]

CGI was created in 1993 and, for the most part, was a framework for

accepting HTTP calls, serving up static content and calling scripts to return dynamic content results.
[2]

The important parts to remember is that CGI was 100% stateless relative to backend resources.
Each dynamic script called was a new, heavyweight operating system process and new connection
to the database. Java programs were shoehorned into this framework as scripts.

12.2. JavaEE
Jakarta EE, formerly the Java Platform, Enterprise Edition (JavaEE) and Java 2 Platform, Enterprise
Edition (J2EE) is a framework that extends the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) to be an
end-to-end Web to database functionality and more.

[3]

Focusing only on the web and database

12.2. JavaEE
Jakarta EE, formerly the Java Platform, Enterprise Edition (JavaEE) and Java 2 Platform, Enterprise
Edition (J2EE) is a framework that extends the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) to be an
end-to-end Web to database functionality and more.

[3]

Focusing only on the web and database
portions here, JakartaEE provided a means to invoke dynamic scripts — written in Java — within a
process thread and cached database connections.
The initial versions of Jakarta EE aimed big. Everything was a large problem and nothing could be
done simply. It was viewed as being overly complex for most users. Spring was formed initially as a
means to make J2EE simpler and ended up soon being an independent framework of its own.
J2EE first was released in 1999 and guided by Sun Microsystems. The Servlet portion was likely the
most successful portion of the early release. The Enterprise Java Beans (EJB) portion was not
realistically usable until JavaEE 5 / post 2006. By then, frameworks like Spring had taken hold of the
target community.
In 2010, Sun Microsystems and control of both JavaSE and JavaEE was purchased by Oracle and
seemed to progress but on a slow path. By JavaEE 8 in 2017, the framework had become very
Spring-like with its POJO-based design. In 2017, Oracle transferred ownership of JavaEE to Jakarta.
The framework seems to have paused for a while for naming changes and compatibility releases.

[3]

12.3. Spring
Spring 1.0 was released in 2004 and was an offshoot of a book written by Rod Johnson "Expert Oneon-One J2EE Design and Development" that was originally meant to explain how to be successful
with J2EE.

[4]

In a nutshell, Rod Johnson and the other designers of Spring thought that rather than starting with
a large architecture like J2EE, one should start with a simple bean and scale up from there without
boundaries. Small Spring applications were quickly achieved and gave birth to other frameworks

Chapter 28. Parent POM
We are likely to create multiple Spring Boot modules and would be well-advised to begin by
creating a local parent pom construct to house the common passive definitions. By passive
definitions (versus active declarations), I mean definitions for the child poms to use if needed
versus mandated declarations for each child module. For example, a parent pom may define the
JDBC driver to use when needed but not all child modules will need a JDBC driver nor a database
for that matter. In that case, we do not want the parent pom to actively declare a dependency. We
just want the parent to passively define the dependency that the child can optionally choose to
actively declare. This construct promotes consistency among all of the modules.

among child poms and use dependencyManagement and pluginManagement
elements to do so.
"Child"/concrete/leaf poms declare dependencies and plugins to be used when
building that module and try to keep dependencies to a minimum.
"Prototype" poms are a blend of root and child pom concepts. They are a nearly-

concrete, parent pom that can be extended by child poms but actively declare a
select set of dependencies and plugins to allow child poms to be as terse as

We saw earlier how we could build a standard executable JAR using the maven-jar-plugin. However,

built with the aid of the spring-boot-maven-plugin. Lets extend our pom.xml file to enhance the
standard JAR to be a Spring Boot executable JAR.

31.1.1. Declare spring-boot-maven-plugin

addition to building the Spring Boot executable JAR, we are setting up a standard in the parent for
all children to have their follow-on JAR classified separately as a bootexec. classifier is a core
Maven construct and is meant to lable sibling artifacts to the original Java JAR for the module.
Other types of classifiers are source, schema, javadoc, etc. bootexec is a value we made up.
By default, the repackage goal would have replaced the Java JAR with the Spring Boot executable

its JAR type. This will help eliminate dependency errors during the semester when we layer N+1
assignments on top of layer N. Only standard Java JARs can be used in classpath dependencies.

Chapter 41. Dependency Injection
Our AppCommand class has been defined only with the interface to Hello and not a specific
implementation.
This Separation of Concerns helps improve modularity, testability, reuse, and many other desirable
features of an application. The interaction between the two classes is defined by an interface.
But how do does our client class (AppCommand) get an instance of the implementation (StdOutHello)?
• If the client class directly instantiates the implementation — it is coupled to that specific
implementation.

public AppCommand() {
this.greeter = new StdOutHello("World");
}
• If the client class procedurally delegates to a factory — it runs the risk of violating Separation of
Concerns by adding complex initialization code to its primary business purpose

public AppCommand() {
this.greeter = BeanFactory.makeGreeter();
}
Traditional procedural code normally makes calls to libraries in order to perform a specific
purpose. If we instead remove the instantiation logic and decisions from the client and place that
elsewhere, we can keep the client more focused on its intended purpose. With this inversion of
control (IoC), the application code is part of a framework that calls the application code when it is
time to do something versus the other way around. In this case the framework is for application
assembly.
Most frameworks, including Spring, implement dependency injection through a form of IoC.

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
public class AppCommand implements CommandLineRunner {
//@Autowired -- FIELD injection ③
private Hello greeter;
@Autowired //-- Constructor injection ①
public AppCommand(Hello greeter) {

//@Autowired -- PROPERTY injection ②
public void setGreeter(Hello hello) {
this.greeter = hello;

① constructor injection - injected values required prior to instance being created
② field injection - value injected directly into attribute
③ setter or property injection - setter() called with value

42.1. @Autowired Annotation
The @Autowired(required=…) annotation
• may be applied to fields, methods, constructors
• @Autowired(required=true) - default value for required attribute
◦ successful injection mandatory when applied to a property
◦ specific constructor use required when applied to a constructor
▪ only a single constructor per class may have this annotation
• @Autowired(required=false)
◦ injected bean not required to exist when applied to a property
◦ specific constructor an option for container to use
◦ multiple constructors may have this annotation applied
▪ container will determine best based on number of matches
◦ single constructor has an implied @Autowired(required=false) - making annotation
optional
There are more details to learn about injection and the lifecycle of a bean. However, know that we

• The only constructor requires a Hello instance

Chapter 56. Property File Source(s)
Spring Boot uses three key properties when looking for configuration files (Ref: docs.spring.io):
1. spring.config.name — one or more base names separated by commas. The default is application
and the suffixes searched for are .properties and .yml (or .yaml)
2. spring.profiles.active — one or more profile names separated by commas used in this context
to identify which form of the base name to use. The default is default and this value is located at
the end of the base filename separated by a dash (-; e.g., application-default)
3. spring.config.location — one or more directories/packages to search for configuration files or
explicit references to specific files. The default is:
a. file:config/ - within a config directory in the current directory
b. file:./ - within the current directory
c. classpath:/config/ - within a config package in the classpath
d. classpath:/ — within the root package of the classpath
Names are primarily used to identify the base name of the application (e.g., application or myapp) or
of distinct areas (e.g., database, security). Profiles are primarily used to supply variants of property
values. Location is primarily used to identify the search paths to look for configuration files but can
be used to override names and profiles when a complete file path is supplied.

Chapter 61. Introduction
In the previous chapter we mapped properties from different sources and then mapped them
directly into individual component Java class attributes. That showed a lot of power but had at least

Chapter 64. Constructor Binding
The previous example was a good start. However, I want to create a slight improvement at this
point with a similar example and make the JavaBean read-only. This better depicts the contract we
have with properties. They are read-only.
To accomplish a read-only JavaBean, we should remove the setter(s), create a custom constructor
that will initialize the attributes at instantiation time, and ideally declare the attributes as final to
enforce that they get initialized during construction and never changed.
The only requirement Spring places on us is to add a @ConstructorBinding annotation to the class or
constructor method when using this approach.
Constructor Binding Example

...
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConstructorBinding;
@ConfigurationProperties("app.config.boat")
public class BoatProperties {
private final String name; ③
@ConstructorBinding ②
public BoatProperties(String name) {
this.name = name;
}
//no setter method(s) ①
public String getName() {
return name;
}
@Override
public String toString() {
return "BoatProperties{name='" + name + "\'}";
}
}
① remove setter methods to better advertise the read-only contract of the bean
② add custom constructor and annotate the class or constructor with @ConstructorBinding
③ make attributes final to better enforce the read-only nature of the bean

Chapter 65. Validation
The error in the last example would have occurred whether we used constructor or setter-based
binding. We would have had a possibly vague problem if the property was needed by the
application. We can help detect invalid property values for both the setter and constructor
approaches by leveraging validation.
Java validation is a JavaEE/ Jakarta EE standard API for expressing validation for JavaBeans. It
allows us to express constraints on JavaBeans to help further modularize objects within our
application.
To add validation to our application, we start by adding the Spring Boot validation starter (springboot-starter-validation) to our pom.xml.

<dependency>
<groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>

• jakarta.validation-api - this is the validation API and is required to compile the module
• hibernate-validator - this is a validation implementation
• tomcat-embed-el - this is required when expressing validations using regular expressions with
@Pattern annotation

Chapter 73. Introduction
Thus far we have focused on how to configure an application within the primary application
module, under fairly static conditions, and applied directly to a single application.
However, our application configuration will likely be required to be:
• dynamically determined - Application configurations commonly need to be dynamic based on
libraries present, properties defined, resources found, etc. at startup. For example, what
database will be used when in development, integration, or production? What security should
be enabled in development versus production areas?
• modularized and not repeated - Breaking the application down into separate components and
making these components reusable in multiple applications by physically breaking them into
separate modules is a good practice. However, that leaves us with the repeated responsibility to
configure the components reused. Many times there could be dozens of choices to make within
a component configuration and the application can be significantly simplified if an opinionated
configuration can be supplied based on the runtime environment of the module.
If you find yourself needing configurations determined dynamically at runtime or find yourself
solving a repeated problem and bundling that into a library shared by multiple applications, you
are going to want to master the concepts within Spring Boot’s Auto-configuration capability that
will be discussed here. Some of these Auto-configuraton capabilities mentioned can be placed
directly into the application while others are meant to be placed into separate Auto-configuration
modules called "starter" modules that can come with an opinionated, default way to configure the
component for use with as little work as possible.

An Auto-configuration class is technically no different than any other @Configuration class except
that it is inspected after the User-defined @Configuration class(es) processing is complete and based
on being named in a META-INF/spring.factories descriptor. This alternate identification and second

Chapter 82. Class Conditions
There are many conditions we can add to our @Configuration class or methods. However, there is an
important difference between the two.
• class conditional annotations prevent the entire class from loading when not satisfied
• @Bean factory conditional annotations allow the class to load but prevent the method from being
called when not satisfied
This works for missing classes too! Spring Boot parses the conditional class using ASM to detect and
then evaluate conditions prior to allowing the class to be loaded into the JVM. Otherwise we would
get a ClassNotFoundException for the import of a class we are trying to base our condition on.

82.1. Class Conditional Example
In the following example, I am adding @ConditionalOnClass annotation to prevent the class from
being loaded if the implementation class does not exist on the classpath.

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@ConditionalOnClass(StdOutHello.class) ②
@EnableConfigurationProperties(HelloProperties.class)
public class HelloAutoConfiguration {
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
public Hello hello(HelloProperties helloProperties) {
return new StdOutHello(helloProperties.getGreeting()); ①
}
}
① StdOutHello is the implementation instantiated by the @Bean factory method
② HelloAutoConfiguration.class will not get loaded if StdOutHello.class does not exist

The sibling @ConditionalOnMissingClass accepts only the string form of the classname.

Chapter 86. Introduction
86.1. Why log?
Logging has many uses within an application — spanning:
• auditing actions
• reporting errors
• providing debug information to assist in locating a problem
With much of our code located in libraries — logging is not just for our application code. We will
want to know audit, error, and debug information in our library calls as well:
• did that timer fire?
• which calls failed?
• what HTTP headers were input or returned from a REST call?

86.2. Why use a Logger over System.out?
Use of Loggers allow statements to exist within the code that will either:
• be disabled
• log output uninhibited
• log output with additional properties (e.g., timestamp, thread, caller, etc.)
Logs commonly are written to the console and/or files by default — but that is not always the case.
Logs can also be exported into centralized servers or database(s) so they can form an integrated
picture of a distributed system and provide search and alarm capabilities.



However simple or robust your end logs become, logging starts with the code and
is a very important thing to include from the beginning (even if we waited a few
modules to cover it).

86.3. Goals
The student will learn:
• to understand the value in using logging over simple System.out.println calls
• to understand the interface and implementation separation of a modern logging framework
• the relationship between the different logger interfaces and implementations
• to use log levels and verbosity to properly monitor the application under different
circumstances

• to express valuable context information in logged messages
• to manage logging verbosity
• to configure the output of logs to provide useful information

89.4. Getting a Logger
Logging frameworks make use of the fundamental design idiom — separate interface from
implementation. We want our calling code to have simple access to a simple interface to express
information to be logged and the severity of that information. We want the implementation to have
limitless capability to produce and manage the logs, but want to only pay for what we likely will
use. Logging frameworks allow that to occur and provide primary access thru a logging interface
and a means to create an instance of that logger. The following diagram shows the basic stereotype
roles played by the factory and logger.

• Factory creates Logger

Chapter 90. Logging Levels
The

Logger

from

the

LoggerFactory

have

an

associated

level

assigned

elsewhere — that represents its verbosity threshold. We issue messages to the Logger using separate
methods that indicate their severity.

Figure 15. Logging Level

The logging severity level calls supported by SLF4J span from trace() to error(). The logging
threshold levels supported by Spring Boot and Logback also span from TRACE to ERROR and include
an OFF (all levels are case insensitive). When we compare levels and thresholds — treat TRACE being
less (severe) than ERROR.



Severity levels supported by other APIs ( JUL Levels, Log4J2 Levels) are mapped
to levels supported by SLF4J.

90.1. Common Level Use
Although there cannot be enforcement of when to use which level — there are common
conventions. The following is a set of conventions I live by:
TRACE
Detailed audits events and verbose state of processing
• example: Detailed state at a point in the code. SQL, params, and results of a query.
DEBUG
Audit events and state giving insight of actions performed
• example: Beginning/ending a decision branch or a key return value
INFO
Notable audit events and state giving some indication of overall activity performed
• example: Started/completed transaction for purchase

211

<!-- page 258 -->
WARN
Something unusual to highlight but the application was able to recover
• example: Read timeout for remote source
ERROR
Significant or unrecoverable error occurred and an important action failed. These should be
extremely limited in their use.
• example: Cannot connect to database

90.2. Log Level Adjustments
Obviously, there are no perfect guidelines. Adjustments need to be made on a case by case basis.




When forming your logging approach — ask yourself "are the logs telling me what
I need to know when I look under the hood?", "what can they tell me with different
verbosity settings?", and "what will it cost in terms of performance and storage?".
The last thing you want to do is to be called in for a problem and the logs tell you
nothing or too much of the wrong information. Even worse — changing the
verbosity of the logs will not help for when the issue occurs the next time.

Chapter 91. Discarded Message Expense
The designers of logger frameworks are well aware that excess logging — even statements that are
disabled — can increase the execution time of a library call or overall application. We have already
seen how severity level thresholds can turn off output and that gives us substantial savings within
the logging framework itself. However, we must be aware that building a message to be logged can
carry its own expense and be aware of the tools to mitigate the problem.
Assume we have a class that is relatively expensive to obtain a String representation.
Example Expensive toString()

class ExpensiveToLog {
public String toString() { ①
try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (Exception ignored) {}
return "hello";
}
}
① calling toString() on instances of this class will incur noticeable delay

91.1. Blind String Concatenation
Now lets say we create a message to log through straight, eager String concatenation. What is wong
here?
Blind String Concatenation Example

ExpensiveToLog obj=new ExpensiveToLog();
//...
log.debug("debug for expensiveToLog: " + obj + "!");
1. The log message will get formed by eagerly concatenating several Strings together
2. One of those Strings is produced by a relatively expensive toString() method
3. Problem: The work of eagerly forming the String is wasted if DEBUG is not enabled

log.debug("debug for expensiveToLog: " + obj + "!");
1. The log message will get formed by eagerly concatenating several Strings together
2. One of those Strings is produced by a relatively expensive toString() method
3. Problem: The work of eagerly forming the String is wasted if DEBUG is not enabled
91.2. Verbosity Check
Assuming the information from the toString() call is valuable and needed when we have DEBUG
enabled — a verbosity check is one common solution we can use to determine if the end result is
worth the work. There are two very similar ways we can do this.
The first way is to dynamically check the current threshold level of the logger within the code and
only execute if the requested severity level is enabled. We are still going to build the relatively
expensive String when DEBUG is enabled but we are going to save all that processing time when it is
not enabled. This overall approach of using a code block works best when creating the message
requires multiple lines of code. This specific technique of dynamically checking is suitable when

there are very few checks within a class.

91.2.1. Dynamic Verbosity Check
The first way is to dynamically check the current threshold level of the logger within the code and
only execute if the requested severity level is enabled. We are still going to build the relatively
expensive String when DEBUG is enabled but we are going to save all that processing time when it is
not enabled. This overall approach of using a code block works best when creating the message
requires multiple lines of code. This specific technique of dynamically checking is suitable when
there are very few checks within a class.
Dynamic Verbosity Check Example

if (log.isDebugEnabled()) { ①
log.debug("debug for expensiveToLog: " + obj +"!");
}
① code block with expensive toString() call is bypassed when DEBUG disabled

91.2.2. Static Final Verbosity Check
A variant of the first approach is to define a static final boolean variable at the start of the class,
equal to the result of the enabled test. This variant allows the JVM to know that the value of the if
predicate will never change allowing the code block and further checks to be eliminated when
disabled. This alternative is better when there are multiple blocks of code that you want to make
conditional on the threshold level of the logger. This solution assumes the logger threshold will
never be changed or that the JVM will be restarted to use the changed value. I have seen this
technique commonly used in libraries where they anticipate many calls and they are commonly
judged on their method throughput performance.

Each of the previous examples showed logging output using a particular pattern. The pattern was

93.7. Conversion Pattern Specifiers
Spring Boot Features Web Page documents some formatting rules. However, more details on the
parts within the conversion pattern are located on the Logback Pattern Layout Web Page. The
overall end-to-end pattern definition I have shown you is called a "Conversion Pattern". Conversion
Patterns are made up of:
• Literal Text (e.g., ---, whitespace, :) — hard-coded strings providing decoration and spacing for
conversion specifiers
• Conversion Specifiers - (e.g., %-40.40logger{39}) — an expression that will contribute a formatted
property of the current logging context
◦ starts with %
◦ followed by format modifiers — (e.g., -40.40) — addresses min/max spacing and right/left
justification
▪ optionally provide minimum number of spaces
▪ use a negative number (-#) to make it left justified and a positive number (#) to make
it right justified
▪ optionally provide maximum number of spaces using a decimal place and number (.#).
Extra characters will be cut off
▪ use a negative number (.-#) to start from the left and positive number (.#) to start
from the right

◦ followed by a conversion word (e.g., logger, msg) — keyword name for the property
◦ optional parameters (e.g., {39}) — see individual conversion words for details on each
