So we can conclude that **`event.target` is always the element that triggered the event**. **`target` vs `currentTarget`:** - `event.target` = what was actually clicked (the deepest element) - `event.currentTarget` = the element the listener is attached to

## 53. Event Propagation: Bubbling & Capturing

> **When an event occurs on a DOM element, that event does not occur entirely on just that
> one element.** It travels through the DOM tree. Event propagation describes how an event
> should flow in the DOM tree.

### The three phases

**1. Capturing Phase (a.k.a. trickling)**
The event starts from the `window` and goes **down** through every ancestor element until it
reaches the target element.

**2. Target Phase**
The event has reached the target element — the element where the event was triggered. Any
event handlers associated with the target element for that event execute in this phase.

**3. Bubbling Phase**
The event **bubbles up** from the target element and goes up through every ancestor element
until it reaches the `window` again.

```
                    CAPTURING ↓            BUBBLING ↑
        window            1                     6
          │               ↓                     ↑
        <div>             2                     5
          │               ↓                     ↑
        <div>             3                     4
          │               ↓                     ↑
       <button>  ←──── 3.5 TARGET PHASE ────→
```

### Controlling the phase

**The 3rd argument of `addEventListener()` controls this:**
- `false` (the **default**) → the handler runs in the **BUBBLING** phase
- `true` → the handler runs in the **CAPTURING** phase

```javascript
element.addEventListener("click", handler);          // bubbling (default)
element.addEventListener("click", handler, false);   // bubbling (explicit)
element.addEventListener("click", handler, true);    // capturing
```

## 54. Event Delegation

> **Event delegation is a technique in JavaScript where a SINGLE event listener is attached to
> a PARENT element instead of attaching event listeners to multiple child elements.**

The event object has a special property called **`.target`** which helps us get access to the
individual child elements.

### Why it matters

Imagine a list with 1,000 items. Without delegation you'd attach 1,000 listeners — slow and
memory-hungry. And if you add a new item later, it would have **no listener at all**.

With delegation, you attach **one** listener to the parent. It catches every click that
bubbles up, and `event.target` tells you which child was actually clicked. **New children
work automatically**, because the parent listener was always there.

## 56. Form Validation

> **It is important to validate the form submitted by the user, because it can have
> inappropriate values. So validation is a must to authenticate the user.**

JavaScript provides the facility to validate the form on the **client side**, so data
processing will be **faster than server-side validation**. Most web developers prefer
JavaScript form validation.

Through JavaScript we can validate name, password, email, date, mobile numbers and more.

> ⚠️ **Client-side validation is for user experience only.** It makes the form feel fast and
> friendly. **You must ALWAYS validate on the server too**, because a malicious user can
> disable JavaScript entirely.

## 57. Cookies

> **A cookie is an amount of information that persists between a server-side and a
> client-side. A web browser stores this information at the time of browsing.**

A cookie contains the information as a **string**, generally in the form of a **name-value
pair separated by semicolons**. It maintains the state of a user and remembers the user's
information among all the web pages.

### How cookies work

- When a user sends a request to the server, each of those requests is treated as a **new
  request sent by a different user** (HTTP is stateless).
- So, to recognise the old user, we need to **add the cookie with the response from the
  server**, which is stored in the browser at the client side.
- Now, whenever a user sends a request to the server, **the cookie is added with that request
  automatically**. Due to the cookie, the server recognises the user.

### Cookie attributes

JavaScript provides some optional attributes that enhance the functionality of cookies.

| Attribute | Description |
|---|---|
| **`expires`** | Maintains the state of a cookie up to the specified date and time |
| **`max-age`** | Maintains the state of a cookie up to the specified time, **in seconds** |
| **`path`** | Expands the scope of the cookie to all pages of a website |
| **`domain`** | Specifies the domain for which the cookie is valid |
| `secure` | Only send over HTTPS |
| `SameSite` | Controls cross-site sending (`Strict` / `Lax` / `None`) |

## 58. Web Storage: localStorage & sessionStorage

A modern, far easier alternative to cookies for storing data **in the browser**.

| | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | **Persists even after the browser closes** | **Cleared when the tab/window is closed** |
| Scope | Shared across all tabs of the same origin | That one tab only |
| Capacity | ~5–10 MB | ~5–10 MB |
| Sent to server? | ❌ Never | ❌ Never |

Compare with cookies: ~4KB max, and **sent with every HTTP request**.

## 60. The Event Loop

The Event Loop is the mechanism that makes single-threaded JavaScript feel multi-tasking.

### The pieces

```
    ┌─────────────────── JavaScript Engine ────────────────────┐
    │                                                           │
    │   ┌────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐         │
    │   │  Call Stack    │        │  Message Queue   │         │
    │   │ Last-in        │        │ (Task Queue)     │         │
    │   │ First-out      │        │ [Task][Task][..] │         │
    │   │                │        └──────────────────┘         │
    │   │ Execution Ctx  │              ↑                       │
    │   │ Execution Ctx  │              │                       │
    │   │ Global Ex.Ctx  │              │                       │
    │   └────────────────┘              │                       │
    │           ↑                        │                      │
    │           └──── EVENT LOOP ────────┘                      │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    ↑
                        ┌───────────┴─────────────┐
                        │   Third-Party Processes │
                        │   • HTTP Process        │
                        │   • Timer Process       │
                        │   • DOM Events          │
                        └─────────────────────────┘
```

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| **Call Stack** | Where functions actually execute. Last-in, first-out. |
| **Web APIs / third-party processes** | The browser handles timers, HTTP requests, DOM events — **outside** the JS thread. |
| **Message Queue (Task Queue)** | Finished callbacks wait here (`setTimeout`, DOM events). |
| **Microtask Queue** | Higher priority queue for **Promise** callbacks. |
| **Event Loop** | Constantly checks: *"Is the call stack empty? If so, move the next queued task onto it."* |

### The golden rule

> **The Event Loop only moves a queued callback onto the call stack when the call stack is
> COMPLETELY EMPTY.**

That's why `setTimeout(fn, 0)` doesn't run immediately — it has to wait for all your
synchronous code to finish first.

### Microtasks beat macrotasks

**Promises** go into the **microtask queue**, which is drained **before** the task queue.

```javascript
console.log('1');

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);       // macrotask

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));  // microtask

console.log('4');

// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
```

**Why?**
1. `1` — synchronous
2. `setTimeout` callback → task queue
3. `.then` callback → **microtask** queue
4. `4` — synchronous
5. Stack empty → drain **microtasks first** → `3`
6. Then the task queue → `2`

Understanding this one example means you understand the event loop.

---

## 62. Promises

> **A Promise is an object that provides a useful construct when dealing with asynchronous
> tasks. It is called a "Promise" because it guarantees it will run upon success or failure
> of that task.**

Or in the words of the handwritten notes:

> *Promises in real life express a trust between two or more people and an assurance that a
> particular thing will surely happen. In JavaScript, a Promise is an object which ensures to
> produce a single value in the future. Promises in JavaScript are used for managing and
> tackling asynchronous operations.*

**A Promise represents a value that will be available now, later, or never.**

### The four states of a Promise

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **pending** | The initial state — neither rejected nor fulfilled yet |
| **fulfilled** | The related promise action was **fulfilled successfully** |
| **rejected** | The related promise action **failed** to be fulfilled |
| **settled** | Either the action is fulfilled **or** rejected — i.e. it's done |

Thus a promise represents the completion of an asynchronous operation with its result. It can
be either successful completion, or its failure, but eventually completed. A Promise uses
`.then()`, which is executed only after the promise resolves.

text:
### The three guarantees a Promise makes

1. Unless the current execution of the JS event loop is completed (success or failure),
   callbacks will **never** be called before it.
2. Even if the callbacks with `.then()` are present, they will be called **only after the
   asynchronous operation completes**.
3. When multiple callbacks are included by invoking `.then()` many times, **each of them will
   be executed in a chain** — one after the other, following the sequence in which they were
   inserted.

text:
### The method summary

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `resolve(value)` | Mark the promise as successful and pass a result |
| `reject(error)` | Mark the promise as failed and pass an error message |
| `.then(cb)` | Handle the successful result of a resolved promise |
| `.catch(cb)` | Handle the error if the promise gets rejected |
| `.finally(cb)` | Run code after the promise is settled — no matter success or failure |
| `Promise.resolve(v)` | Create an already-resolved promise |
| `Promise.reject(e)` | Create an already-rejected promise |

### Chaining — the cure for callback hell

**Each `.then()` returns a new Promise**, so you can chain them into a flat sequence.
One `.catch()` at the end handles errors from **any** step.

```javascript
getUser(userId)
  .then(user    => getOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders  => getOrderDetails(orders[0].id))
  .then(details => getShipping(details.shippingId))
  .then(shipping => console.log(shipping))
  .catch(error   => console.error("Something failed:", error));  // ONE handler for all
```

Compare that to the pyramid of doom above. Flat, readable, one error path.

> ⚠️ **You must `return` inside `.then()`**, otherwise the next `.then()` receives `undefined`.

---

text:
### `Promise.race([...])` — first one to settle wins

Resolves or rejects as soon as the **first** promise settles — success **or** failure.

```javascript
Promise.race([fetchData(), timeout(5000)])
  .then(value => console.log(value));
```

**Use when:** implementing timeouts.
```javascript
const timeout = ms => new Promise((_, rej) =>
  setTimeout(() => rej(new Error('Timed out')), ms));

const data = await Promise.race([fetch(url), timeout(5000)]);
```

### `Promise.any([...])` — first SUCCESS wins

Ignores rejections. Only rejects if **every** promise rejects.

```javascript
const fastest = await Promise.any([mirror1(), mirror2(), mirror3()]);
```

### Quick comparison

| Method | Resolves when | Rejects when |
|---|---|---|
| `all` | **All** succeed | **Any** one fails |
| `allSettled` | All settle | **Never** |
| `race` | **First** settles | First settles as a rejection |
| `any` | **First** succeeds | **All** fail |

### Running things in PARALLEL

> ⚠️ **The most common `async/await` performance mistake:** awaiting things one after
> another when they don't depend on each other.

```javascript
// ❌ SLOW — sequential. Total time = 1s + 1s = 2 seconds
const a = await fetchA();     // waits 1s
const b = await fetchB();     // then waits another 1s

// ✅ FAST — parallel. Total time = 1 second
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]);
```

Only await sequentially when step 2 genuinely needs step 1's result.

### Rules and gotchas

- `await` only works **inside an `async` function** (or at the top level of an ES module).
- An `async` function **always** returns a Promise, even if you return a plain value.
- Forgetting `await` gives you the Promise object itself, not the value:
  ```javascript
  const data = fetch(url);          // ❌ a Promise object
  const data = await fetch(url);    // ✅ the actual Response
  ```
- Unhandled rejections in async functions produce warnings. Always `try/catch` or `.catch()`.

### The three async styles compared

| Style | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Callbacks** | Simple for one level | ❌ Callback hell; error handling repeated |
| **Promises** | ✅ Cleaner than callbacks; chainable | ❌ Can still get messy with many `.then()` |
| **async/await** | ✅ Very clean and readable; normal try/catch | ❌ Must be used inside an `async` function |

---

### The older XMLHttpRequest

You'll still see this in legacy code:
```javascript
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open('GET', url);
xhr.send();
```
`fetch` replaced it. Use `fetch`.

# PART 8 — ERRORS, MODULES & ADVANCED

---

## 66. Error Handling

> **In programming, exception handling is a process or method used for handling the abnormal
> statements in the code and executing them. It also enables you to handle the flow control
> of the code/program.**

In exception handling:
- A **`throw`** statement is used to raise an exception. When an abnormal condition occurs, an
  exception is thrown using `throw`.
- The thrown exception is handled by wrapping the code into the **`try`** block.

### The three types of errors

While coding, there can be three types of errors in the code:

**1. Syntax Error**
When a user makes a mistake in the predefined syntax of a programming language, a syntax error
may appear. The code won't even run.
```javascript
let x = ;          // SyntaxError
```

**2. Runtime Error**
When an error occurs **during the execution** of the program, such an error is known as a
runtime error. The codes which create runtime errors are known as **Exceptions**. Thus,
exception handlers are used for handling runtime errors.
```javascript
undefinedFunction();     // ReferenceError at runtime
```

**3. Logical Error**
An error which occurs when there is a **logical mistake** in the program, that may not produce
the desired output, and may terminate abnormally. **The hardest to find** — the code runs
perfectly, it just gives the wrong answer.
```javascript
function average(a, b) { return a + b / 2; }   // ⚠️ missing parentheses — wrong maths
```

### The 7 built-in error types

Although `Error` is a generic constructor, there are the following standard built-in error
types (error constructors) beside it:

| Error type | When it happens |
|---|---|
| **EvalError** | An error that occurred in the `eval()` global function, used for evaluating JS string code |
| **InternalError** | Created when the JS engine throws an internal error |
| **RangeError** | A numeric variable or parameter is **out of its valid range** |
| **ReferenceError** | An **invalid reference** is de-referenced (using an undeclared variable) |
| **SyntaxError** | A syntax error that may occur while parsing |
| **TypeError** | A variable is **not a valid type** |
| **URIError** | Invalid parameters passed in `encodeURI()` or `decodeURI()` |

```javascript
new Array(-1);          // RangeError: Invalid array length
undefinedVariable;      // ReferenceError: undefinedVariable is not defined
null.property;          // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
decodeURI('%');         // URIError: URI malformed
```

## 67. Debugging

> **Sometimes a code may contain mistakes. Being a scripting language, JavaScript doesn't
> show any error message in a browser. But these mistakes can affect the output.**

### Method 1 — using `console.log()`

The `console.log()` method displays the result in the console of the browser. If there is any
mistake in the code, it generates the error message.

```javascript
x = 10;
y = 15;
z = x + y;
console.log(z);     // 25
console.log(a);     // ⚠️ ReferenceError — 'a' is not initialised
```

**Better console methods for debugging:**
```javascript
console.table([{a:1,b:2}, {a:3,b:4}]);   // pretty table — great for arrays of objects
console.group('Label'); console.log('nested'); console.groupEnd();
console.time('op'); /* ...work... */ console.timeEnd('op');   // measure duration
console.count('clicked');                 // how many times did this run?
console.trace();                          // where was this called from?
console.assert(x > 0, 'x should be positive');
```

### Method 2 — using the `debugger` keyword

In debugging, we generally set **breakpoints** to examine each line of code step by step.
**There is no requirement to perform this task manually in JavaScript** — just write
`debugger;` and the browser pauses there (as long as DevTools is open).

```javascript
x = 10;
y = 15;
z = x + y;
debugger;              // ← execution pauses here
document.write(z);
document.write(a);
```

While paused you can inspect every variable, and step through with:
- **Step over** — run the next line
- **Step into** — go inside the function being called
- **Step out** — finish the current function and come back
- **Resume** — continue until the next breakpoint

### Method 3 — DevTools breakpoints

Open DevTools → **Sources** tab → click a line number to set a breakpoint. No code change
needed. This is what professionals use.

### A debugging strategy

1. **Read the actual error message.** It tells you the type, the message, the file and the line.
2. **Check the line above** the reported one — errors often surface one line late.
3. **`console.log` the variables** just before the failure. Is the value what you expected?
4. **Check the type**, not just the value: `console.log(typeof x, x)`.
5. **Comment out half** the code. Does the bug persist? Now you know which half to search.
6. **Use `debugger`** to freeze time and look around.

**The most common beginner errors:**

| Error | Usual cause |
|---|---|
| `Cannot read properties of null` | `getElementById` found nothing — check the ID, or move the `<script>` to the bottom |
| `Cannot read properties of undefined` | You accessed a property on something that doesn't exist |
| `x is not a function` | Typo, or `x` isn't what you think it is |
| `x is not defined` | Typo in the variable name, or it's out of scope |
| `Unexpected token` | A missing bracket, brace or comma |
| `Maximum call stack size exceeded` | Infinite recursion — you forgot the base case |

---

### Named vs default — the difference

| | Named export | Default export |
|---|---|---|
| How many per file | Many | **One** |
| Import syntax | `import { x } from` | `import x from` |
| Name must match? | ✅ Yes (unless renamed with `as`) | ❌ No — call it anything |

### Requirements

> **Note:** Modules require a server environment or specific browser configuration.

```html
<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>
```

- You **must** use `type="module"`
- File extensions are required in the browser: `'./math.js'` not `'./math'`
- Modules are **always in strict mode** automatically
- Modules are **deferred** by default (they wait for the HTML to parse)
- Because of CORS, you need to serve over `http://`, not open the file directly with `file://`
  (use VS Code's Live Server, or `npx serve`)

## 73. Other Web APIs

Web APIs are features provided **by the browser**, not by the JavaScript language itself.

## 73. Other Web APIs

Web APIs are features provided **by the browser**, not by the JavaScript language itself.
| API | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Web Storage** | Persistent (`localStorage`) and session (`sessionStorage`) storage in browser memory | `localStorage.setItem('k','v')` |
| **Fetch** | Make HTTP calls | `fetch(url).then(r => r.json())` |
| **Geolocation** | Get the user's location | `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(p => console.log(p))` |
| **Canvas** | Draw 2D/3D graphics | `const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')` |
| **Web Audio** | Create and play sound — e.g. an oscillator playing a tone | `new AudioContext()` |
| **Web Speech** | Text-to-speech and speech recognition | `speechSynthesis.speak(new SpeechSynthesisUtterance("Hello There"))` |
| **WebSockets** | Real-time, bidirectional communication protocol | `new WebSocket('ws://example.com')` |
| **IndexedDB** | Structured client-side data storage (much bigger than localStorage) | `indexedDB.open('db', 1)` |
| **File / FileRea

der** | Manipulate files, access metadata | `reader.readAsDataURL(file)` |
| **Notification** | Display system notifications | `new Notification("Hi!")` |
| **Web Workers** | Execute background scripts off the main thread | `new Worker('worker.js')` |
| **Intersection Observer** | Efficiently observe element visibility changes | Lazy-loading images, infinite scroll |
| **Mutation Observer** | Observe DOM changes asynchronously | `new MutationObserver(cb)` |
| **Pointer Lock** | Capture mouse movements precisely in-browser | Used by browser games |
| **Battery Status** | Monitor device battery information asynchronously | `navigator.getBattery()` |
| **Gamepad** | Interact with game controller devices | `navigator.getGamepads()` |

| **Push** | Enable push notifications in browsers | Service Workers + Push |
| **Payment Request** | Streamlined online payment processing | `new PaymentRequest(...)` |
| **Performance** | Measure timings precisely | `performance.now()` |
| **requestAnimationFrame** | Schedule smooth animations | `requestAnimationFrame(step)` |

### Nullish coalescing `??`

Returns the right-hand side **only if** the left is `null` or `undefined`.

```javascript
let val = obj?.key ?? "Default";
```

**Crucially different from `||`:**
```javascript
0        || "default"    // "default"  ⚠️ 0 is falsy
0        ?? "default"    // 0          ✅ 0 is a real value
""       || "default"    // "default"  ⚠️
""       ?? "default"    // ""         ✅
null     ?? "default"    // "default"  ✅
```

> ✅ **Use `??` for defaults when `0`, `""` or `false` are legitimate values.**

## 75. ES6+ Feature Checklist

The full list of what "modern JavaScript" means.

### ES6 (2015) — the big one

1. **`let`, `const`** (instead of only `var`)
2. **Arrow Functions** `() => {}`
3. **Template Literals** `` `Hello, ${name}` ``
4. **Default Parameters** — used inside functions
5. **Destructuring**
   - Array Destructuring — `let [a, b] = [1, 2];`
   - Object Destructuring — `let { name, age } = person;`
6. **Spread Operator** — `...arr`, `...obj`
7. **Rest Operator** — `...rest`
8. **`for...of` Loop** — new in ES6 for iterating arrays
9. **Set and Map** data structures
10. **Promises** — `.then()`, `.catch()`, `.finally()`
11. **Classes** — `class`, `extends`, `super`, `static`
12. **ES6 Modules** — `export`, `import`
13. **Generators** — `function*`, `yield`
14. **Symbols**
15. **Proxy & Reflect**

### ES2017+
- **`async` / `await`** (ES2017)
- **Object spread in objects** (ES2018)
- **`Array.flat()` / `flatMap()`** (ES2019)
- **`Object.fromEntries()`** (ES2019)
- **`String.trimStart()` / `trimEnd()`** (ES2019)
- **Optional chaining `?.`** (ES2020)
- **Nullish coalescing `??`** (ES2020)
- **BigInt** (ES2020)
- **`Promise.allSettled()`** (ES2020)
- **Dynamic `import()`** (ES2020)
- **Logical assignment `||=` `&&=` `??=`** (ES2021)
- **`String.replaceAll()`** (ES2021)
- **`Promise.any()`** (ES2021)
- **Class private fields `#`** (ES2022)
- **Top-level `await`** (ES2022)
- **`Array.at()`** (ES2022)
- **`Object.hasOwn()`** (ES2022)
- **`Array.toSorted()` / `toReversed()` / `with()`** — non-mutating (ES2023)
- **`Array.findLast()` / `findLastIndex()`** (ES2023)

**And the Web API you must know:** `fetch` — modern HTTP requests, built on Promises.

### The one-line summary

> `let`, `const`, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest operators,
> `for...of`, Set, Map, Promises, `async`/`await`, the fetch API, and ES6 modules.

# PART 9 — PRACTICE

## 76. Full Project: A To-Do List Application

This project pulls together everything you've learned:

- **DOM Manipulation**
- **Event Handling**
- **Local Storage for persistence**
- **Basic Array methods** (`map`, `filter`, `push`, `forEach`)
- **Functions**

The application lets users **add, delete, and mark tasks as complete**, with tasks
**persisting across browser sessions**.

Save this as a single `.html` file and open it in a browser.

### What to notice in this code

| Concept | Where it appears |
|---|---|
| **Selecting elements** | `document.getElementById(...)` at the top |
| **Arrays as state** | `let tasks = []` — the single source of truth |
| **Array methods** | `push` (add), `map` (toggle), `filter` (delete), `forEach` (render) |
| **Spread operator** | `{ ...task, completed: !task.completed }` — copy then override |
| **JSON** | `stringify` to save, `parse` to load |
| **localStorage** | Persistence across browser sessions |
| **Creating elements** | `createElement` + `appendChild` |
| **Event listeners** | `addEventListener` on buttons and the input |
| **Arrow functions + closures** | `() => toggleComplete(task.id)` captures `task.id` |
| **XSS safety** | `textContent` rather than `innerHTML` for user input |
| **`DOMContentLoaded`** | Wait for the HTML before touching the DOM |

## 77. Learning Roadmap

### The five levels

**Level 1 — Beginner (Weeks 1–2)**
Variables · data types · operators · `if`/`else` · loops · functions · basic arrays and
objects · `console.log`
> ✅ **Milestone:** write a program that takes numbers and prints the largest one.

**Level 2 — DOM & Events (Weeks 3–4)**
Selecting elements · changing text and styles · `addEventListener` · form validation ·
creating and removing elements
> ✅ **Milestone:** build a working to-do list (section 76).

**Level 3 — Intermediate (Weeks 5–7)**
`map`/`filter`/`reduce` · destructuring · spread/rest · template literals · arrow functions ·
scope · hoisting · **closures** · `this`
> ✅ **Milestone:** explain closures and `this` to someone else without notes.

**Level 4 — Asynchronous (Weeks 8–10)**
Callbacks · Promises · `async`/`await` · `fetch` · the event loop · error handling
> ✅ **Milestone:** build an app that fetches data from a public API and displays it,
> with loading and error states.

**Level 5 — Advanced (Weeks 11+)**
Prototypes · classes and OOP · modules · generators · Proxy · design patterns ·
performance · testing
> ✅ **Milestone:** you can read any JavaScript codebase and understand what it does.

### The 20-hour Pareto plan (10 × 2-hour sessions)

The 20% of JavaScript that generates 80% of the results:

| # | Focus | Ends with |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Variables, data types, operators, truthy/falsy | Type quiz — predict `typeof` for 15 values |
| 2 | Conditionals, loops, `break`/`continue` | FizzBuzz; multiplication table |
| 3 | Functions, parameters, arrow functions, scope | Write 5 reusable utility functions |
| 4 | Arrays + `map`/`filter`/`reduce` | Transform an array of user objects 5 ways |
| 5 | Objects, destructuring, spread/rest | Model a shopping cart with objects |
| 6 | DOM selection and manipulation | Build a colour-changing page |
| 7 | Events, forms, validation | Build a validated sign-up form |

### The 10 mistakes beginners make

1. Using `var` instead of `let`/`const`
2. Using `==` instead of `===`
3. Forgetting `return` inside a function or a `.then()`

### The six questions to ask on any async problem

| Question | If yes, reach for |
|---|---|
| Multiple callers want the same thing at the same time? | Deduplication — `Map` + shared promise |
| Does each step depend on the previous result? | Async recursion, or sequential `await` |
| Can things run independently at the same time? | `Promise.all(items.map(...))` |
| Can it loop back on itself forever? | Depth counter, or a visited `Set` |
| Must it fail fast if too slow? | `Promise.race([work, timeout])` |
| Can it fail temporarily but succeed on retry? | Retry with exponential backoff |

text:
### Data structure quick pick

| Structure | Use for |
|---|---|
| `Map` | Cache of key → in-flight promise. Dedup, memoisation. `.has()` `.get()` `.set()` `.delete()` |
| `Set` | Visited IDs, loop detection. O(1) `.has()` |
| `Array` | Collecting promises for `Promise.all` via `.map()` |
| Object | Structured output — `Object.keys()` + `Object.fromEntries()` |

### The eight async mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `await` inside a plain `for` loop | Everything runs sequentially, slowly | `Promise.all` + `.map()` |
| Forgetting the argument — `apiCall()` | Returns `data-undefined` | `apiCall(id)` |
| Cache declared **inside** the function | Cache resets every call; dedup never works | Move it outside |
| Storing the *result* instead of the *promise* | Duplicate calls fire before the first resolves | Store the promise object |
| `.finally()` for cache cleanup | Timing issues — cache not cleared in time | Use `.then(fn, fn)` |
| Unhandled promise rejection | Node crashes | `.catch()` on every chain |
| No base case in recursion | Stack overflow, infinite loop | Check the exit condition first |
| Forgetting to re-throw in `.catch()` | Error swallowed; caller thinks it succeeded | `catch(err => { cleanup(); throw err; })` |

### Unhandled rejections crash Node

A rejected promise with no `.catch()` terminates a Node process. When you keep a side reference to a
promise, suppress the crash on the side chain while letting the returned promise carry the real error:

```javascript
const promise = apiCall(id);
promise.catch(() => {});      // suppress the unhandled-rejection crash
return promise;               // the caller still receives the real rejection
```

## Q1. What's the difference between `undefined` and `null`?

**`undefined`** is the **default value** of:
- a variable that has not been assigned a specific value
- a function that has no explicit return value (e.g. `console.log(1)`)
- a property that does not exist in an object

**The JavaScript engine does this for us** — it assigns the `undefined` value automatically.

**`null`** is **"a value that represents no value"**. It is a value that has been **explicitly
defined** by *you*. For example, you get `null` when `fs.readFile` does not throw an error.

```javascript
let a;
console.log(a);              // undefined — JS assigned it

let b = null;
console.log(b);              // null — I assigned it

console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);        // "object"  ⚠️ a famous historical bug

console.log(null == undefined);  // true  — loose equality says they're alike
console.log(null === undefined); // false — different types
```

> **One-line answer:** `undefined` means "JavaScript hasn't given this a value yet".
> `null` means "I deliberately set this to nothing".

---

## Q2. What is the DOM? **DOM stands for Document Object Model.** It is an **interface (an API)** for HTML and XML documents. When the browser first reads (parses) our HTML document, it creates a big object — a really big object — based on the HTML document. **This is the DOM.** It is a **tree-like structure** that is modelled from the HTML document. The DOM is used for interacting with and modifying the DOM structure, or specific Elements or Nodes. The **`document`** object in JavaScript represents the DOM. It provides many methods we can use to select elements, update element contents, and much more. ```html DOM

``` Becomes: ``` document └── html ├── head → title └── body → div → p → span → label → input ```

## Q3. What is Event Propagation?

**When an event occurs on a DOM element, that event does not entirely occur on that just one
element.**

- In the **Bubbling Phase**, the event bubbles up: it goes to its parent, to its grandparent,
  to its grandparent's parent, until it reaches all the way to the `window`.
- In the **Capturing Phase**, the event starts from the `window` and goes down to the element
  that triggered the event — the `event.target`.

**Event Propagation has three phases:**

1. **Capturing Phase** — the event starts from `window`, then goes down through every element
   until it reaches the target element.
2. **Target Phase** — the event has reached the target element.
3. **Bubbling Phase** — the event bubbles up from the target element, then goes up through
   every element until it reaches the `window`.

```
CAPTURING ↓                              BUBBLING ↑
window  →  html  →  body  →  div  →  [TARGET]  →  div  →  body  →  html  →  window
```

**Controlling it:** the third argument of `addEventListener()` decides the phase.
```javascript
el.addEventListener('click', fn);          // false (default) = BUBBLING
el.addEventListener('click', fn, true);    // true            = CAPTURING
```

Use `e.stopPropagation()` or `e.stopImmediatePropagation()` to stop it.

## Q7. What's the difference between `==` and `===`?

**The difference between `==` (abstract equality) and `===` (strict equality) is that `==`
compares by value AFTER COERCION, and `===` compares by value AND TYPE WITHOUT COERCION.**

**Coercion** is the process of converting a value to another type. The `==` operator does
**implicit coercion**.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q7. What's the difference between `==` and `===`?

text:
### The `==` algorithm

Suppose we compare `x == y`:

1. If `x` and `y` have the **same type**, compare them with the `===` operator.
2. If `x` is `null` and `y` is `undefined`, return **`true`**.
3. If `x` is `undefined` and `y` is `null`, return **`true`**.
4. If `x` is type **number** and `y` is type **string**, return `x == toNumber(y)`.
5. If `x` is type **string** and `y` is type **number**, return `toNumber(x) == y`.
6. If `x` is type **boolean**, return `toNumber(x) == y`.
7. If `y` is type **boolean**, return `x == toNumber(y)`.
8. If `x` is `string`/`symbol`/`number` and `y` is type **object**, return `x == toPrimitive(y)`.
9. If `x` is **object** and `y` is `string`/`symbol`, return `toPrimitive(x) == y`.
10. Otherwise return **`false`**.

> **Note:** `toPrimitive` uses first the `valueOf` method, then the `toString` method, to get
> the primitive value of that object.

### Examples with `==` — these all return `true`

| x | y | `x == y` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `5` | `5` | `true` | Condition 1 — same type and value |
| `1` | `'1'` | `true` | Condition 4 — `y` converted to a number |
| `null` | `undefined` | `true` | Condition 2 |
| `0` | `false` | `true` | Condition 7 — `y` is boolean, becomes `0` |
| `'1,2'` | `[1,2]` | `true` | Condition 8 — the array became `"1,2"` via `toString()` |
| `'[object Object]'` | `{}` | `true` | Condition 10 path — the object became `"[object Object]"` |

### The same examples with `===`

| x | y | `x === y` |
|---|---|---|
| `5` | `5` | **`true`** |
| `1` | `'1'` | `false` |
| `null` | `undefined` | `false` |
| `0` | `false` | `false` |
| `'1,2'` | `[1,2]` | `false` |
| `'[object Object]'` | `{}` | `false` |

**If we use the `===` operator, all the comparisons except for the first example return
`false`**, because they don't have the same type. The first returns `true` because the two
have the same type and value.

> ✅ **Always use `===`.** The only common exception is `x == null`, which conveniently checks
> for both `null` and `undefined` at once.

## Q8. What is Hoisting?

**Hoisting is the term used to describe the moving of variables and functions to the top of
their (global or function) scope, where we define that variable or function.**

To understand hoisting, you have to understand the **execution context**.

**The Execution Context is the "environment of code" that is currently executing.** It has
**two phases: compilation and execution.**

**Compilation phase** — it gets all the **function declarations** and hoists them up to the
top of their scope, so we can reference them later. It also gets all **variables declared with
the `var` keyword**, hoists them up, and gives them a default value of **`undefined`**.

**Execution phase** — it assigns values to the variables hoisted earlier, and it executes or
invokes functions (methods in objects).

> **⚠️ Note: ONLY function declarations and variables declared with the `var` keyword are
> hoisted — NOT function expressions, arrow functions, `let`, or `const`.**

### What about `let` and `const`?

They **are** hoisted, but placed in the **Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)** — accessing them before
their declaration throws a `ReferenceError` rather than giving `undefined`.

```javascript
console.log(a);   // undefined ✅
var a = 1;

console.log(b);   // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 1;
```

---

## Q9. What are Closures?

**Closures is simply the ability of a function at the time of DECLARATION to remember the
references of variables and parameters on its current scope, on its parent function scope, on
its parent's parent function scope, until it reaches the global scope — with the help of the
Scope Chain. Basically it is the Scope created when the function was declared.**

## Q10. What's the value of `this` in JavaScript?

**Basically, `this` refers to the value of the object that is currently executing or invoking
the function.** We say "currently" because **the value of `this` changes depending on the
context in which we use it, and where we use it.**

text:
### Now let's make it weird

Add these three lines below the `console.log` statement:

```javascript
var name = "Ford Ranger";
var getCarName = carDetails.getName;

console.log(getCarName());   // logs "Ford Ranger"
```

**The second `console.log` prints `"Ford Ranger"`, which is weird**, because the first
printed `"Ford Mustang"`.

**The reason:** the `getCarName` method has a **different "owner" object — the `window`
object**. Declaring variables with the `var` keyword in the global scope attaches properties
to the `window` object with the same name as the variables. **Remember, `this` in the global
scope refers to the `window` object when `"use strict"` is not used.**

```javascript
console.log(getCarName === window.getCarName);   // logs true
console.log(getCarName === this.getCarName);     // logs true
```
`this` and `window` in this example refer to the same object.

### Solving it with `apply` and `call`

```javascript
console.log(getCarName.apply(carDetails));   // logs "Ford Mustang"
console.log(getCarName.call(carDetails));    // logs "Ford Mustang"
```

**The `apply` and `call` methods expect the first parameter to be an object, which becomes the
value of `this` inside that function.**

### Summary table

| How it's called | `this` is |
|---|---|
| Plain function | `window` (or `undefined` in strict mode) |
| Method `obj.fn()` | `obj` |
| `new Fn()` | The new instance |
| Arrow function | Inherited from the enclosing lexical scope |
| `fn.call/apply/bind(x)` | `x` |
| Event handler | The element that received the event |

## Q12. Why are functions called First-class Objects?

**Functions in JavaScript are First-class Objects because they are treated as any other value
in the language.** They can be:

- **assigned to variables**
- **properties of an object** — which are then called **methods**
- **an item in an array**
- **passed as arguments** to a function
- **returned as values** of a function

**The ONLY difference between a function and any other value in JavaScript is that functions
can be INVOKED or CALLED.**

```javascript
const fn = function() {};              // assigned to a variable
const obj = { method: function() {} }; // a property → a method
const arr = [function() {}];           // an item in an array
[1,2].map(function(x) { return x; });  // passed as an argument
function outer() { return function() {}; }  // returned as a value
```

### So how do we know it uses prototypes under the hood?

```javascript
class Something { }
function AnotherSomething(){ }

const as = new AnotherSomething();
const s  = new Something();

console.log(typeof Something);          // logs "function"
console.log(typeof AnotherSomething);   // logs "function"
console.log(as.toString());             // logs "[object Object]"
console.log(s.toString());              // logs "[object Object]"
console.log(as.toString === Object.prototype.toString);   // true
console.log(s.toString  === Object.prototype.toString);   // true
```

**Both logs return `true`, indicating that we are still using prototypes under the hood** —
because `Object.prototype` is the last part of the Prototype Chain, and both `Something` and
`AnotherSomething` inherit from `Object.prototype`.

## Q17 & Q19. What is a Callback function?

**A Callback function is a function that is going to get called at a later point in time.**

```javascript
const btnAdd = document.getElementById('btnAdd');

btnAdd.addEventListener('click', function clickCallback(e) {
  // do something useless
});
```

In this example, we wait for the `click` event on the element with an id of `btnAdd`. **If it
is clicked, the `clickCallback` function is executed.**

**A Callback function adds some functionality to some data or event.** The `reduce`, `filter`
and `map` methods in Array expect a callback as a parameter.

> **A good analogy for a callback:** when you call someone and they don't answer, you leave a
> message and you expect them to **call back**. The act of calling someone or leaving a
> message is the **event or data**, and the **callback is the action that you expect to occur
> later**.

---

In JavaScript, handling asynchronous operations is essential when working with tasks like API
calls, file reading, timers, or any operations that take time to complete. JavaScript provides
several ways to manage async code efficiently:

text:
# SECTION B — Rapid-Fire Questions

Short, common questions with short answers.

### Q. What is JavaScript?
A high-level, interpreted, lightweight, dynamically-typed, single-threaded, case-sensitive
programming language used to add interactivity and logic to web pages. Runs in browsers and,
via Node.js, on servers.

### Q. Who created JavaScript and what was it first called?
**Brendan Eich**, a Netscape programmer, created it in **just 10 days in September 1995**. It
was first called **Mocha**, then **LiveScript**, then **JavaScript** (a marketing decision
because Java was popular).

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. Who created JavaScript and what was it first called?

text:
### Q. Is JavaScript the same as Java?
**No.** They are completely different languages with nothing in common but four letters in the
name.

### Q. What is ECMAScript?
The **official specification** that JavaScript implements, maintained by **Ecma
International** (founded 1996). ES1 was released in 1997. **ES6 (2015)** was the biggest
update. Since 2015, TC39 releases a new version **annually**.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. Is JavaScript the same as Java?

text:
### Q. What are the data types in JavaScript?
**Primitive (7):** String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null, Symbol, BigInt.
**Non-primitive:** Object (and its subtypes Array, Function, RegExp, Date).

### Q. What does `typeof null` return, and why?
`"object"`. It's a **bug** from the original 1995 implementation that can never be fixed
without breaking existing websites.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. What are the data types in JavaScript?

text:
### Q. Difference between `var`, `let` and `const`?

| | Scope | Re-declare | Re-assign | Hoisted as |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| `var` | Function | ✅ | ✅ | `undefined` |
| `let` | Block | ❌ | ✅ | TDZ (error) |
| `const` | Block | ❌ | ❌ | TDZ (error) |

`const` prevents **reassignment**, not **mutation** — you can still change an object's
properties.

### Q. What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
The period between entering a block and the `let`/`const` declaration being executed.
Accessing the variable in this window throws a `ReferenceError`.

### Q. What are the falsy values?
`false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. **Everything else is truthy** —
including `[]` and `{}`.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. What is the Temporal Dead Zone?

text:
### Q. What is coercion?
The automatic conversion of one type to another. Priority order: **String → Number →
Boolean**. `2 + "7"` gives `"27"`; `true - 5` gives `-4`.

### Q. `slice()` vs `splice()`?
`slice(start, end)` returns a copy, **doesn't mutate**.
`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` removes/inserts, **mutates**, returns what it removed.

### Q. `map()` vs `forEach()`?
`map` returns a **new array** of the same length and is chainable.
`forEach` returns `undefined` and is used for side effects only.

### Q. `find()` vs `filter()`?
`find` returns the **first matching element** (or `undefined`).
`filter` returns a **new array of all matches** (possibly empty).

### Q. `some()` vs `every()`?
`some` → `true` if **at least one** passes. `every` → `true` only if **all** pass.

### Q. Why does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` give `[1, 10, 9]`?
By default `sort()` converts elements to **strings** and sorts lexicographically.
Fix: `sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

### Q. Shallow copy vs deep copy?
**Shallow** copies only the top level; nested objects are still shared by reference
(`{...obj}`, `Object.assign`, `slice`).
**Deep** copies everything (`structuredClone(obj)`, or `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` —
which loses functions, dates and `undefined`).

### Q. `null` vs `undefined` vs `NaN`?
`undefined` = not assigned. `null` = deliberately empty. `NaN` = "Not a Number", the result of
an invalid maths operation. `typeof NaN` is `"number"`, and `NaN !== NaN`.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. Shallow copy vs deep copy?

text:
### Q. How do you check for `NaN`?
`Number.isNaN(x)` — the strict version. Avoid the global `isNaN()`, which coerces first
(`isNaN("hello")` is `true`).

### Q. Arrow function vs regular function?

| | Regular | Arrow |
|---|---|---|
| `this` | Own binding, depends on call site | **Lexical** — inherited |
| `arguments` object | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Usable as constructor (`new`) | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Hoisted (declaration form) | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Good as an object method | ✅ Yes | ❌ **No** |

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. How do you check for `NaN`?

text:
### Q. What is an IIFE and why use one?
An **Immediately Invoked Function Expression** — `(function(){ })();`. It runs instantly and
creates a **private scope**, avoiding global namespace pollution. Before ES6 modules and
`let`, this was the main encapsulation tool.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. What is an IIFE and why use one?

text:
### Q. What is `use strict`?
A directive that makes JavaScript stricter: undeclared variables throw, reserved words are
blocked, duplicate parameters are illegal, `this` is `undefined` in plain functions, and some
silent failures become errors. **Modules and classes are strict automatically.**

### Q. What is the Event Loop?
The mechanism that lets single-threaded JavaScript handle async work. Long tasks are handed to
browser Web APIs; their callbacks queue up; the **Event Loop moves a queued callback onto the
call stack only when the stack is empty**. **Microtasks (Promises) are drained before
macrotasks (`setTimeout`).**

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. What is the Event Loop?

text:
### Q. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` — does it run immediately?
**No.** It runs after all synchronous code finishes and the call stack is empty. It's the
*minimum* delay, not a guarantee.

### Q. What are the states of a Promise?
**pending**, **fulfilled**, **rejected** — and **settled** (meaning either fulfilled or
rejected).

### Q. `Promise.all` vs `allSettled` vs `race` vs `any`?

| | Resolves when | Rejects when |
|---|---|---|
| `all` | All succeed | Any one fails |
| `allSettled` | All settle | **Never** |
| `race` | First settles | First settles as a rejection |
| `any` | First succeeds | All fail |

### Q. Does `fetch()` reject on a 404?
**No.** It only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves. You must check
`response.ok` yourself.

### Q. What is a prototype?
An object that other objects inherit properties and methods from. Every object has an internal
`[[Prototype]]` link. Looking up a property walks this **prototype chain** until it finds the
property or reaches `null`.

### Q. `call` vs `apply` vs `bind`?
`call(thisArg, a, b)` — invokes now, comma-separated args.
`apply(thisArg, [a, b])` — invokes now, **array** of args.
`bind(thisArg)` — **returns a new function** with `this` locked; doesn't invoke.

### Q. What is event delegation and why is it useful?
Attaching **one** listener to a parent instead of many to children, then using `event.target`
to identify what was clicked. **Better performance**, and it **automatically works for
elements added later**.

### Q. `innerHTML` vs `textContent` vs `innerText`?
`innerHTML` parses HTML — **XSS risk with user input**.
`textContent` gets/sets all text including hidden — **safe and fast**.
`innerText` respects CSS, so it excludes hidden text and triggers a reflow — slower.

### Q. localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?

| | Lifetime | Size | Sent to server |
|---|---|---|---|
| `localStorage` | Until manually cleared | ~5–10MB | ❌ |
| `sessionStorage` | Until the tab closes | ~5–10MB | ❌ |
| Cookies | Until `expires`/`max-age` | ~4KB | ✅ Every request |

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?

text:
### Q. `==` vs `===` in one line?
`==` compares after **type coercion**; `===` compares **value and type** with no coercion.
Always use `===`.

### Q. What is a pure function?
A function that (1) always returns the same output for the same input, and (2) has **no side
effects** — it doesn't modify anything outside itself.

### Q. What's the difference between an HTMLCollection and a NodeList?
`getElementsByClassName`/`TagName` return a **live** HTMLCollection (updates with the DOM).
`querySelectorAll` returns a **static** NodeList (a snapshot). Neither is a real array —
`NodeList` has `forEach`, `HTMLCollection` doesn't. Use `[...collection]` to convert.

metadata.title: JAVASCRIPT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: Q. What's the difference between an HTMLCollection and a NodeList?

text:
### Q. What is currying?
Transforming a function of many arguments into a chain of single-argument functions:
`f(a, b, c)` → `f(a)(b)(c)`. Useful for partial application.
```javascript
const add = a => b => a + b;
add(2)(3);   // 5
```

### Q. What is debouncing vs throttling?
**Debounce** — wait until the user *stops* firing events, then run once (search-as-you-type).
**Throttle** — run at most once every N milliseconds (scroll, resize handlers).

# PART A — NODE.JS

## A1. What is Node.js

Node.js is an **open-source, cross-platform runtime environment** for developing server-side and networking applications. Node.js applications are written in JavaScript and run inside the Node.js runtime on OS X, Microsoft Windows and Linux.

The key idea:

```
Node.js = JavaScript Runtime Environment + JavaScript Library
```

A browser runs JavaScript to make web pages interactive. Node takes the same JavaScript language and lets it run **outside the browser**, on a server, where it can read files, talk to databases and answer HTTP requests.

### The 7 features of Node.js (from page 1–2)

1. **Extremely fast** — built on Google Chrome's **V8** JavaScript engine, so code execution is very fast.
2. **I/O is asynchronous and event driven** — all APIs of the Node.js library are asynchronous (non-blocking). A Node.js based server never waits for an API to return data: it moves to the next API after calling it, and a **notification mechanism of events** helps it get the response from the previous API call.
3. **Single threaded** — Node.js follows a single threaded model with **event looping**.
4. **Highly scalable** — because events help the server respond in a non-blocking way, it is highly scalable. Node uses a single threaded program that can serve a much larger number of requests than a traditional server like Apache HTTP Server.
5. **No buffering** — Node.js applications never buffer any data; they simply **output the data in chunks**.
6. **Open source** — Node.js has a big open source community which has produced many excellent modules to add extra capabilities to Node.js applications.
7. **License** — Node.js is released under the **MIT license**.

### Parts of Node.js (page 3)

The notebook lists the pieces you will meet as you learn:

Buffer · Streaming · DNS · Domain · Global · Net · Modules · Error Handling · Debugger · Console · Cluster · Add-ons · Callback · Crypto

---

## A2. Installing Node.js and your first programs

### What you need (page 3–4)

To develop Node.js applications on Windows you need only two things:

1. **A text editor** — e.g. Notepad, Notepad++, VIM, Sublime Text.
2. **The Node.js binary installer** — download from `https://nodejs.org/en/download/`.

Source files are written in JavaScript and saved with the **`.js`** extension. The Node.js runtime interprets and executes them.

## A3. The Console module (page 6–8)

The console module provides a simple debugging console, like the JavaScript console of a web browser. Three methods are used most:

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `console.log()` | Prints to stdout with a newline. Supports `printf`-style format specifiers. |
| `console.error()` | Prints to stderr with a newline. |
| `console.warn()` | Prints a warning to stderr. |

**`console.log()` with a format specifier:**

```js
console.log('Hello %s', 'JavaTpoint');   // Hello JavaTpoint
```

**`console.error()`:**

```js
console.error(new Error('Hell! This is a wrong method.'));
```

**`console.warn()` with a template literal:**

```js
const name = 'JavaTpoint';
console.warn(`Warning: ${name} is deprecated`);
```

---

## A4. REPL — the interactive shell (page 8–11)

**REPL stands for Read Eval Print Loop.** It is the console/shell where you can type JavaScript and see the result immediately. Node ships with a REPL: just type `node` with no filename.

The four steps in the name:

| Step | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Read** | Reads the user's input, parses it into a JavaScript data structure, and stores it in memory. |
| **Eval** | Takes the data structure and evaluates it. |
| **Print** | Prints the result produced by evaluating the command. |
| **Loop** | Loops the above command until the user presses `Ctrl+C` twice. |

### Simple expressions

```
> 10 + 20 - 5
25
```

### Using variables

```
> x = 10          // prints 10 (assignment without var echoes the value)
10
> var x = 10      // prints undefined (a var declaration evaluates to undefined)
undefined
> var a = 40, b = 60
undefined
> a + b
100
```

This is a classic beginner trap: `var x = 10` prints `undefined` because a *declaration* has no value; `x = 10` prints `10` because an *assignment expression* evaluates to the assigned value.

### The underscore variable

`_` holds the result of the **last** expression:

```
> var x = 10
> var y = 20
> x + y
30
> var sum = _
> console.log(sum)
30
```

### REPL commands (page 10–11)

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl + C` | Terminate the current command |
| `Ctrl + C` (twice) | Terminate the REPL |
| `Ctrl + D` | Terminate the REPL |
| Up / Down arrows | Browse command history and modify previous commands |
| `Tab` | List the current commands / autocomplete |
| `.help` | List all the commands |
| `.break` | Exit from a multi-line expression |
| `.clear` | Exit from a multi-line expression |
| `.save filename` | Save the current REPL session to a file |
| `.load filename` | Load the given file into the current REPL session |

**To exit the REPL: press `Ctrl + C` twice.**

---

## A5. NPM — Node Package Manager (page 11–12)

NPM (Node Package Manager) provides **two main functionalities**:

1. **Online repositories** for Node.js packages/modules, which are searchable on `search.nodejs.org`.
2. A **command line utility** to install Node.js packages, and to do version management and dependency management of Node.js packages.

NPM comes **bundled with Node.js installables** after version **v0.6.3**. To verify:

```bash
npm version
```

### Installing, uninstalling and searching modules

```bash
npm install <ModuleName>        # install a module
npm install express             # e.g. install express
npm uninstall express           # uninstall a module
npm search express              # search for a module
```

---

## A6. Node.js command line options (page 12–15)

### Installing, uninstalling and searching modules

```bash
npm install <ModuleName>        # install a module
npm install express             # e.g. install express
npm uninstall express           # uninstall a module
npm search express              # search for a module
```

| 1 | `-v`, `--version` | Print node's version |
| 2 | `-h`, `--help` | Print node command line options |

stack traces for deprecations |

| 12 | `--trace-warnings` | Print stack traces for process warnings |

| 14 | `--zero-fill-buffers` | Automatically zero-fill all newly allocated Buffer and SlowBuffer instances |

## A7. Global objects (page 15)

Global objects are available in **all modules** — you do not need to `require()` them. They can be used directly.

| Global | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `__dirname` | The name of the **directory** that the currently executing script lives in |
| `__filename` | The **absolute path** of the file being executed, including the filename |

```js
console.log(__dirname);
console.log(__filename);
```

Other globals covered elsewhere in these notes: `console`, `Buffer`, the timer functions, and `process`.

---

## A8. The OS module (page 16–18)

The OS module provides basic operating-system related utility functions. Load it with `var os = require('os')`.

| # | Method | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `os.arch()` | The operating system CPU architecture |
| 2 | `os.cpus()` | An array of objects with information about each CPU/core: model, speed (in MHz), and times (an object with `user`, `nice`, `sys`, `idle`, `irq` in milliseconds) |
| 3 | `os.endianness()` | The endianness of the CPU — `'BE'` for big endian, `'LE'` for little endian |
| 4 | `os.freemem()` | The amount of free system memory in bytes |
| 5 | `os.homedir()` | The home directory of the current user |
| 6 | `os.hostname()` | The hostname of the operating system

|
| 7 | `os.loadavg()` | An array containing the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages |
| 8 | `os.networkInterfaces()` | A list of network interfaces |
| 9 | `os.platform()` | The operating system platform: `'darwin'`, `'win32'`, `'freebsd'`, `'linux'`, `'sunos'` |
| 10 | `os.release()` | The operating system release |
| 11 | `os.tmpdir()` | The operating system's default directory for temporary files |
| 12 | `os.totalmem()` | The total amount of system memory in bytes |
| 13 | `os.type()` | The operating system name: `'Linux'`, `'Darwin'` on OS X, `'Windows_NT'` on Windows |
| 14 | `os.uptime()` | The system uptime in seconds |
| 15 | `os.userInfo([options])` | Information about the currently effective user |

---

## A9. Timers (page 18–20)

Timers are **global** — you do **not** need to `require('timers')`.

### The three timer functions

| Function | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `setImmediate(callback)` | Runs the callback at the end of the current event loop turn |
| `setInterval(callback, delay)` | Runs the callback **repeatedly**, every `delay` milliseconds |
| `setTimeout(callback, delay)` | Runs the callback **once**, after at least `delay` milliseconds |

### The three cancel functions

| Function | Cancels |
|---|---|
| `clearImmediate(immediateObject)` | A `setImmediate` |
| `clearInterval(intervalObject)` | A `setInterval` |
| `clearTimeout(timeoutObject)` | A `setTimeout` |

### Example — `timer1.js`

```js
setInterval(function () {
    console.log('setInterval: Hey! 1 millisecond completed!.');
}, 1000);
```

This prints the message **every second, forever**, until you stop the program with `Ctrl+C`. (Despite the message text, `1000` means 1000 milliseconds = 1 second.)

---

## A10. Errors and error handling (page 20)

Applications running in Node.js will generally experience **four categories of errors**:

1. **Standard JavaScript errors** —
   - `EvalError` — thrown when a call to `eval()` fails
   - `SyntaxError` — thrown in response to improper JavaScript language syntax
   - `RangeError` — thrown when a value is not within an expected range or set of values
   - `ReferenceError` — thrown when using undefined variables
   - `TypeError` — thrown when passing arguments of the wrong type
   - `URIError` — thrown when a global URI handling function is misused
2. **System errors** — triggered by underlying operating system constraints, such as attempting to open a file that does not exist, or attempting to send data over a closed socket.
3. **User-specified errors** — triggered by application code.
4. **Assertion errors** — a special class of error triggered whenever Node.js detects an exceptional logic violation that should never occur; raised by the `assert` module.

## A11. The DNS module (page 21–22)

DNS (Domain Name System) resolves hostnames into IP addresses. Load with `const dns = require('dns')`.

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `dns.getServers()` | Returns an array of IP address strings for the current DNS servers |
| `dns.setServers(servers)` | Sets the IP addresses of the servers to be used when resolving |
| `dns.lookup(hostname[, options], callback)` | Resolves a hostname into the first found A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) record |
| `dns.lookupService(address, port, callback)` | Resolves the given address and port into a hostname and service |
| `dns.resolve(hostname[, rrtype], callback)` | Resolves a hostname into an array of the record types specified by `rrtype` |
| `dns.resolve4(hostname

, callback)` | Resolves IPv4 addresses (A records) |
| `dns.resolve6(hostname, callback)` | Resolves IPv6 addresses (AAAA records) |
| `dns.resolveCname(hostname, callback)` | Resolves CNAME records |
| `dns.resolveMx(hostname, callback)` | Resolves mail exchange records |
| `dns.resolveNs(hostname, callback)` | Resolves name server records |
| `dns.resolveSoa(hostname, callback)` | Resolves a start of authority record |
| `dns.resolveSrv(hostname, callback)` | Resolves service records |
| `dns.resolvePtr(hostname, callback)` | Resolves pointer records |
| `dns.resolveTxt(hostname, callback)` | Resolves text queries |
| `dns.reverse(ip, callback)` | Performs a reverse DNS query — resolves an IPv4/IPv6 address to hostnames |

## A12. The Net module — socket programming (page 22–23)

The Net module is used to create both **servers and clients**. It provides an asynchronous network wrapper and is what you use for socket programming — for example a chat application, where a server and a client talk to each other.

You need **two command prompts** to run this example: one for the server and one for the client.

## A13. The Crypto module (page 24–26)

The crypto module provides **cryptographic functionality**: it is a set of wrappers for OpenSSL's hash, HMAC, cipher, decipher, sign and verify functions.

**Definitions from the notes:**
- **Hash** — a fixed-length string of bits generated from a piece of data. It is **deterministic**: the same input always produces the same hash.
- **HMAC** — Hash-based Message Authentication Code. It is the result of running a hash algorithm over data **plus a secret key**, so only someone with the key can produce or verify it.

## A14. TLS / SSL (page 26–28)

**TLS = Transport Layer Security**, the successor of **SSL (Secure Socket Layer)**. TLS/SSL is a **public-key cryptography** based protocol. It encrypts the connection at the **TCP layer**.

### How public-key cryptography works (page 27)

- Each client and each server has a **public key** and a **private key**.
- The **public key is shared**; the **private key is kept secret**.
- To send an encrypted message you use **your own private key** together with the **recipient's public key**.
- To read a message you decrypt it with **your own private key**.

Load the module with `const tls = require('tls')`.

## A15. The Debugger (page 29)

Node.js includes a **debugging utility** accessed by a built-in debugging client. The Node.js debugger client is not a full-featured debugger, but simple stepping and inspection are possible. It uses a **TCP based protocol**.

Usage:

```bash
node debug [script.js | -e "script" | <host>:<port>]
```

Example:

```bash
node debug main.js
```

Output starts with:

```
< Debugger listening on port 5858
```

---

## A16. The Process object (page 29–31)

`process` is a **global object**, an instance of **EventEmitter**, that gives information about — and control over — the current Node.js process. It can be accessed from anywhere without `require`.

Typical uses listed in the notes: get process information (pid, architecture, platform, version, release, uptime, CPU usage), **kill** a process, **set uid**, **set groups**, **set umask**.

### Process properties

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| `process.arch` | The processor architecture: `'arm'`, `'ia32'`, `'x64'` |
| `process.args` | An array containing the command line arguments |
| `process.env` | An object containing the user environment |
| `process.pid` | The PID of the process |
| `process.platform` | `'darwin'`, `'freebsd'`, `'linux'`, `'sunos'`, `'win32'` |
| `process.release` | Metadata for the current node release |
| `process.version` | The Node.js version |
| `process.versions` | The Node.js version **and its dependencies** |

Example:

```js
console.log(`Process Architecture: ${process.arch}`);
console.log(`Process PID: ${process.pid}`);
console.log(`Process Platform: ${process.platform}`);
console.log(`Process Version: ${process.version}`);
```

### Process functions

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `process.cwd()` | Returns the path of the current working directory |
| `process.hrtime()` | Returns the current high-resolution real time in a `[seconds, nanoseconds]` array |
| `process.memoryUsage()` | Returns an object having information of memory usage |
| `process.kill(pid[, signal])` | Kills the process of the given pid |
| `process.uptime()` | Returns the Node.js process uptime in seconds |

---

## A18. Buffers (page 34–36)

### Why buffers exist

Pure JavaScript is Unicode friendly but **not nice to binary data**. When dealing with TCP streams or the file system, it is necessary to handle **octet streams**. Node provides a `Buffer` class to store raw data. A buffer is similar to an array of integers, but it corresponds to a **raw memory allocation outside the V8 heap**.

The `Buffer` class is a **global** class — it can be accessed without importing the buffer module.

### Writing to a buffer

```
buf.write(string[, offset][, length][, encoding])
```

- `string` — the string data to be written to the buffer
- `offset` — index of the buffer to start writing at, default `0`
- `length` — number of bytes to write, default `buffer.length`
- `encoding` — default `'utf8'`

It returns the **number of octets written**.

```js
buf = new Buffer(256);
len = buf.write("Simply Easy Learning");
console.log("Octets written : " + len);
```

### Reading from a buffer

```
buf.toString([encoding][, start][, end])
```

```js
buf = new Buffer(26);
for (var i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    buf[i] = i + 97;              // 97 is the char code of 'a'
}

console.log(buf.toString('ascii'));        // abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz
console.log(buf.toString('ascii', 0, 5));  // abcde
console.log(buf.toString('utf8', 0, 5));   // abcde
console.log(buf.toString(undefined, 0, 5));// abcde  (encoding defaults to utf8)
```

---

## A19. Streams (page 37–39)

**Streams are objects that let you read data from a source or write data to a destination in a continuous fashion.**

### The four types of stream

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Readable** | Stream which is used for read operations |
| **Writable** | Stream which is used for write operations |
| **Duplex** | Stream which can be used for both read and write operations |
| **Transform** | A type of duplex stream where the output is computed based on the input |

**Each type of stream is an `EventEmitter` instance** and throws several events at different times.

### Commonly used stream events

| Event | Fired when |
|---|---|
| `data` | Data is available to read |
| `end` | There is no more data to read |
| `error` | There is any error receiving or writing data |
| `finish` | All the data has been flushed to the underlying system |

## A20. The File System (fs) module (page 39–43)

Node implements file I/O using **simple wrappers around standard POSIX functions**. Import it with:

```js
var fs = require("fs");
```

### Synchronous vs asynchronous — the most important idea

**Every method in the fs module has a synchronous and an asynchronous form.**

- **Asynchronous methods** take the **last parameter as a completion function callback**, and the **first parameter of the callback is an error**.
- It is **better to use the asynchronous method** instead of the synchronous one, because the asynchronous method **never blocks the program execution**, whereas the synchronous one does.

### Opening a file

```
fs.open(path, flags[, mode], callback)
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `r` | Open file for reading. **Exception** occurs if the file does not exist |
| `r+` | Open file for reading and writing. Exception occurs if the file does not exist |
| `rs` | Open file for reading in synchronous mode |
| `rs+` | Open file for reading and writing, asking the OS to open it synchronously. Use with caution |
| `w` | Open file for writing. The file is **created** (if it does not exist) or **truncated** (if it exists) |
| `wx` | Like `w` but **fails if the path exists** |
| `w+` | Open file for reading and writing. Created if it does not exist, truncated if it exists |
| `wx+` | Like `w+` but fails if the path exists |
| `a` | Open file for **appending**. The file is created if it does not exist |
| `ax` | Like `a` but fails if the path exists |
| `a+` | Open file for reading and appending. Created if it does not exist |
| `ax+` | Like `a+` but fails if the path exists |

```js
var fs = require("fs");

fs.open('input.txt', 'r+', function (err, fd) {
    if (err) {
        return console.error(err);
    }
    console.log("File opened successfully!");
});
```

## A21. The Path module (page 44–45)

The Path module is used to **handle and transform file paths**.

```js
var path = require("path");
```

| # | Method | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `path.normalize(p)` | Normalizes a string path, taking care of `'..'` and `'.'` parts |
| 2 | `path.join([path1][, path2][, ...])` | Joins all arguments together and normalizes the resulting path |
| 3 | `path.resolve([from ...], to)` | Resolves `to` to an absolute path |
| 4 | `path.isAbsolute(path)` | Determines whether `path` is an absolute path |
| 5 | `path.relative(from, to)` | Solves the relative path from `from` to `to` |
| 6 | `path.dirname(p)` | Returns the directory name of a path — similar to the Unix `dirname` command |
| 7 | `path.basename(p[, ext])` | Returns the last portion of

## A26. The V8 module (page 50–52)

**V8** is an open-source JavaScript engine developed by the Chromium project for Google Chrome. It is **written in C++** and is used in Couchbase, MongoDB and Node.js.

The V8 module in Node exposes interfaces specific to the V8 version built into the Node binary:

```js
const v8 = require('v8');
```

### `v8.getHeapStatistics()`

Returns statistics about the V8 heap: total heap size, used heap size, heap size limit and total available size.

Sample output:

```js
{
  total_heap_size: 8304512,
  total_heap_size_executable: 5242880,
  total_physical_size: 8304512,
  total_available_size: 1491075504,
  used_heap_size: 4289960,
  heap_size_limit: 1535115264
}
```

### `v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics()`

Returns an **array of 5 objects**, one per heap space: `new_space`, `old_space`, `code_space`, `map_space`, `large_object_space`. Each object contains `space_name`, `space_size`, `space_used_size`, `space_available_size`, `physical_space_size`.

### Memory limit of V8 in Node.js

- By default: **512 MB on 32-bit** systems and **1 GB on 64-bit** systems.
- The limit can be raised with **`--max-old-space-size`**, up to roughly **1 GB on 32-bit** and **1.7 GB on 64-bit**.
- If you are hitting memory limits, it is **recommended to split your single process into several workers** rather than keep raising the limit.

---

## A27. Callbacks — blocking vs non-blocking (page 52–53)

**A callback is the asynchronous equivalent of a function.** It is called at the completion of a given task. **All the APIs of Node are written in a way that they support callbacks.**

For example, when a function starts reading a file, it **returns control to the execution environment immediately** so that the next instruction can be executed. In Node.js, once the file I/O is complete, the callback function is called with the file contents. So there is **no blocking or waiting** for file I/O — this makes Node.js **highly scalable**, since it can process a high number of requests without waiting for any function to return results.

### Blocking code example

`input.txt`:

```
JavaTpoint is a website for learning technologies.
```

`main.js`:

```js
var fs = require("fs");

var data = fs.readFileSync('input.txt');

console.log(data.toString());
console.log("Program Ended");
```

Output:

```
JavaTpoint is a website for learning technologies.
Program Ended
```

## A28. Events and event-driven programming (page 54–56)

### Why events

Events and callbacks in Node.js provide **concurrency**. Since Node.js applications are **single threaded** and every API is **asynchronous**, Node uses asynchronous functions to maintain concurrency. Node uses the **Observer pattern**: the Node thread keeps an **event loop**, and after the completion of any task it fires the corresponding event, which signals the event listener function to execute.

### Event-driven programming

As soon as Node starts its server, it simply **initiates its variables, declares functions and then waits for an event to occur**. This is one of the reasons Node.js is fast compared to other similar technologies. In an event-driven application there is generally a **main loop that listens for events, and then triggers a callback function when one of those events is detected**.

The flow:

```
EventEmitters  --->  Events  --->  Event Loop  --->  Event Handlers
```

## A29. Punycode (page 56–58)

**Punycode is an encoding syntax which is used to convert a Unicode (UTF-8) string of characters to a basic ASCII string of characters.** Since **host names only understand ASCII characters**, Punycode is used for that conversion. It is used as **Internationalized Domain Name (IDN or IDNA — Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications)**.

Punycode.js is **bundled with Node.js v0.6.2 and later**. To use it with an older version: `npm install punycode`, then `const punycode = require('punycode')`.

| Method | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `punycode.decode(string)` | Converts a Punycode string of ASCII symbols to a Unicode string | `punycode.decode('maana-pta')` → `mañana` |
| `punycode.encode(string)` | Converts a Unicode string to a Punycode ASCII string | `punycode.encode('mañana')` → `maana-pta` |
| `punycode.toASCII(domain)` | Converts a Unicode domain name to Punycode — **only the non-ASCII parts are converted** | `punycode.toASCII('mañana.com')` → `xn--maana-pta.com` |
| `punycode.toUnicode(domain)` | Converts a Punycode domain name to Unicode — only the punycoded parts are converted | `punycode.toUnicode('xn--maana-pta.com')` → `mañana.com` |

---

## A30. The TTY module (page 58–60)

The TTY module contains the **`tty.ReadStream`** and **`tty.WriteStream`** classes. In most cases you will not need to use this module directly.

```js
var tty = require('tty');
```

When Node.js is run inside a TTY context:
- **`process.stdin` is a `tty.ReadStream` instance**
- **`process.stdout` is a `tty.WriteStream` instance**

To check whether Node.js is being run in a TTY context:

```bash
node -p -e "Boolean(process.stdout.isTTY)"
```

Output: `true`

### Class `tty.ReadStream`

A subclass of `net.Socket` that represents the **readable portion** of a TTY. Normally the **only instance is `process.stdin`** (and only when `isatty(0)` is true).

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `rs.isRaw` | A Boolean, initialized to `false`. It specifies the current "raw" state of the `tty.ReadStream` instance |
| `rs.setRawMode(mode)` | `mode` should be `true` or `false`. This sets the properties of the `tty.ReadStream` to act as a raw device or as a default device. `isRaw` is set to the resulting mode |

### What is a Web Server

A web server is a **software program which handles the HTTP requests sent by HTTP clients** like web browsers, and returns web pages in response to the clients. Web servers usually respond with **HTML documents** along with images, style sheets and scripts.

### Web application architecture — the four layers

| Layer | Role |
|---|---|
| **Client Layer** | Web browsers, mobile browsers or applications which make the HTTP requests |
| **Server Layer** | The web server which intercepts the requests made by the clients and passes them the response |
| **Business Layer** | The application server utilized by the web server to do the required processing. This layer interacts with the data layer via a database or some external programs |
| **Data Layer** | The database or any source of data |

```
Client (Mobile Browser / Web Browser / Application)
      |
Server (Web Server)
      |
Business Layer (Application Server, File System)
      |
Data Layer (Database, External System)
```
