# PART 17 — Refs, Fragments, Portals, HOCs and Context

## 17.1 Refs

**"Refs" is shorthand for "references".** It is an attribute which makes it possible to store a reference to a particular DOM node or React element. It provides a way to access React DOM nodes or React elements and to interact with them.

metadata.title: REACT-COMPLETE-NOTES
metadata.section: PART 17 — Refs, Fragments, Portals, HOCs and Context

text:
### When to use refs
- When we need **DOM measurements** such as managing focus, text selection, or media playback.
- For triggering **imperative animations**.
- When **integrating with third-party DOM libraries**.
- It can also be used in callbacks.

### When NOT to use refs
- Avoid using refs for anything that can be done **declaratively**. Instead of using `open()` and `close()` methods on a Dialog component, you should pass an `isOpen` prop to it.
- **You should avoid overuse of refs.**

### Accessing refs
When a ref is passed to an element inside the render method, a reference to the node can be accessed via the **`current`** attribute of the ref:
```jsx
const node = this.callRef.current;
```

### The `current` property — three rules
- When the `ref` attribute is used on an **HTML element**, the ref created with `React.createRef()` receives the underlying **DOM element** as its `current` property.
- If the `ref` attribute is used on a **custom class component**, the ref object receives the **mounted instance** of the component as its `current` property.
- **The `ref` attribute cannot be used on a function component** because they don't have instances. *(Use `forwardRef` or, in React 19, ref-as-a-prop.)*

### Callback refs
There is another way to use refs, called **callback refs**, which gives more control over when refs are set and unset. Instead of creating a ref object, you pass a callback function to the `ref` attribute:

```jsx
<input type="text" ref={element => this.callRefInput = element} />
```

The callback function stores a reference to the DOM node in an instance property, which can then be accessed elsewhere:
```jsx
this.callRefInput.value
```

### Why use fragments?
1. **It makes execution of code faster** compared to a `div` tag.
2. **It takes less memory.**
3. It doesn't add an extra node to the DOM — the rendered HTML is cleaner and more efficient, especially when a component renders a list of items.
4. **It helps with accessibility** because it doesn't create an unnecessary wrapper element around the content.

metadata.title: REACT-COMPLETE-NOTES
metadata.section: Can you nest fragments inside fragments?

text:
### Syntax
```jsx
ReactDOM.createPortal(child, container)
```
- **`child`** — a React component or fragment that can be rendered in the DOM.
- **`container`** — a reference to the element present in the HTML page into which the child element will be rendered.

### Features of portals
- It uses **React version 16** and its official API for creating portals.
- It has a fallback for React version 15.
- It transports its children component into a new React portal which is **appended by default to `document.body`**.
- It can also target a **user-specified DOM element**.
- It supports **server-side rendering**.
- It supports returning arrays.
- It **doesn't produce any DOM mess**.
- It has **no dependencies** — minimalistic.
- Flexible component rendering, improved performance, integration with third-party libraries, encapsulation and isolation.

## 17.5 Higher-Order Components (HOC)

**A higher-order component (HOC) is a function that takes a component as an argument and returns a new component with additional functionality.**

HOCs are used to **reuse component logic**, such as authentication or performance optimization.

```jsx
const NewComponent = higherOrderComponent(WrappedComponent);
```

### Render hijacking
**Render hijacking in React is a technique that allows you to modify the rendered output of a component by wrapping it in another component.** The wrapping component can then add or remove elements, change the styles, or modify the behavior of the original component. HOCs are how this is done.

---

## 17.6 The Context API

**The Context API allows passing data through the component tree without passing props down manually at every level.**

It provides a way for components to access data that is **"global" to the component tree**, such as a user's authentication status or a theme. It provides a way to create a **global state** that can be accessed and modified by components at any level.

### The four parts of the Context API

**1. `React.createContext`** — creates a context object.
```jsx
const MyContext = React.createContext(defaultValue);
```

**2. `Context.Provider`** — every Context object has a Provider React component which allows consuming components to subscribe to context changes.
```jsx
<MyContext.Provider value={/* some value */} />
```

**3. `Context.Consumer`** — a React component which subscribes to context changes. It allows us to access the context within a function.
```jsx
<MyContext.Consumer>
  {value => /* render something based on the context value */}
</MyContext.Consumer>
```

**4. `class.contextType`** — the `contextType` property on a class is used to assign a context object created by `React.createContext()`. It allows you to consume the closest current value of that context using `this.context`.

# PART 18 — State Management

## 18.1 Why state management?

**State management in a React application refers to the process of managing and organizing the application's state**, which includes data, UI states, and other relevant information.

As the application grows in complexity, managing state becomes more challenging, and **proper state management techniques are necessary to ensure a predictable and maintainable application.**

There are different approaches:
1. **React Context API** (built in) — see Part 17.6
2. **Redux**
3. Alternatives: **Mobx, Apollo, Unstated-next, Zustand**

---

## 18.2 MVC vs Flux

### MVC (Model View Controller)
MVC is an architectural pattern used for developing the user interface.

- **Model** — responsible for maintaining the behaviour and data of an application.
- **View** — used to display the model in the user interface.
- **Controller** — acts as an interface between the Model and the View. It takes user input, manipulates the data, and causes the view to update.

```
MODEL ──UPDATES──▶ VIEW ──SEES──▶ USER ──USES──▶ CONTROLLER ──MANIPULATES──▶ MODEL
```

### Flux
**Flux is an application architecture that Facebook uses for building client-side web applications.** It is designed to be used with React and it provides a **unidirectional data flow**, where data is passed down through components in a hierarchical structure.

Flux architecture has 3 major roles in dealing with data:
1. **Dispatcher**
2. **Store**
3. **Views**

```
Action ──▶ Dispatcher ──▶ Store ──▶ View ──▶ Action  (loop)
```

- **Action Creator** — a helper method that creates an action from its parameters, assigns it a type, and then provides it to the dispatcher.
- **Dispatcher** — acts as a central hub. It sends every action to all stores via the callbacks that have registered with it.
- **Store** — updates itself in response to an action, then emits a change event to alert the controller view.
- **Controller view** — listens for change events, retrieves new data from the stores, and provides the new data to their descendants in the component tree.

### MVC vs Flux — the comparison

| | MVC | Flux |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduced in **1976** | Introduced just a few years ago |
| 2 | Supports **bi-directional** data flow model | Supports **uni-directional** data flow model |
| 3 | **Data binding** is the key | **Events or actions** are the key |
| 4 | It is **synchronous** | It is **asynchronous** |
| 5 | Controllers handle everything | **Store** handles all logic |
| 6 | It is **hard to debug** | It is **easy to debug** |
| 7 | Difficult to understand as project size increases | Easy to understand |
| 8 | Maintainability is difficult as the project scope grows huge | Maintainability is easy and it reduces run-time errors |
| 9 | Testing of the application is **difficult** | Testing of the application is **easy** |
| 10 | Scalability is complex | It can be easily scaled |

---

## 18.3 Redux

**Redux is a predictable state container for JavaScript applications.** It helps you write apps that behave consistently, run in different environments (client, server, native) and are easy to test.

- Redux is a **state management tool**.
- Redux can be used with **any** JavaScript framework — it is not React-specific.
- Redux stores the state of the application, and components can access the state from the state store.
- It provides a **centralised, predictable and immutable state container**.

**Redux was inspired by Flux.** The differences:
1. Redux does **not** have the dispatcher concept.
2. Redux has **only one Store**, whereas Flux has many stores.
3. Action objects are received and handled **directly by the Store**.

### The Redux architecture
```
Store ──contains──▶ State ──defines──▶ UI ──triggers──▶ Actions ──sent to──▶ Reducer ──updates──▶ Store
```

---

## 18.4 The three principles of Redux

**1. Single Source of Truth**
The state of your whole application is stored in an object tree within a **single store**. A single state tree makes it easier to debug or inspect an application. It gives you a faster development cycle by enabling you to persist your app's navigation state.

**2. State is read-only**
The only way to change the state is to **initiate an action** — an object describing what happened. This ensures that no events like network callbacks or views can change state directly. Actions are just plain objects, so they can be logged.

**3. Changes are made with pure functions**
To specify how actions transform the state tree, you write **pure reducers**. The user can return new state objects instead of mutating previous state.

---

## 18.5 The core concepts of Redux

### Store
**The Redux store holds the application state.** It is created using the `createStore()` function from the Redux library and manages the state and state updates.

A store is a place where the entire state of your application lives. It manages the status of the application and has a dispatch function. **It is like a brain, responsible for all moving parts in Redux.**

Store methods:
- **`getState()`** — returns the current state
- **`dispatch()`** — dispatches an action
- **`subscribe()`** — adds a change listener to state
- **`unsubscribe()`** — stops calling your listener method when state changes

### Actions
**Actions are plain JavaScript objects that represent events or intentions to modify the state.** They have a **`type`** property that describes the action and can also include additional data. Actions are dispatched to the store using the `store.dispatch()` method.

An action is sent or dispatched from the view. Actions are payloads that can be read by Reducers. An action is a pure object created to store the information about a user's event. It includes information such as the type of action, time of occurrence, location of occurrence, its coordinates, and which state it aims to change.

### Reducers
**Reducers are pure functions that specify how the state should change in response to actions.** They take the **current state** and an **action** as arguments and return a **new state**. Reducers define how the state is transformed and updated.

A reducer reads the payload from the action and then updates the store via the state accordingly. It is a pure function that returns a new state from the initial state.

> **Why are Redux state functions called reducers?** Because they are used to **reduce** the current state and an action into the next state. The reducer takes the current state and an action as input and returns the next state.

### Dispatch
**Dispatching an action is the process of sending an action to the store.** Components can dispatch actions using the `dispatch()` method provided by the Redux store.

### Connect
**The `connect()` function is used to connect components to the Redux store.** It allows components to access the state and dispatch actions.

---

## 18.6 Using Redux — step by step

### Step 1 — Install the dependencies
```bash
npm install redux react-redux
```

### Step 2 — Create the Redux store
Use `createStore()` from the Redux library. The store holds the application state and provides methods to dispatch actions and subscribe to changes.

```jsx
import { createStore } from 'redux';
import rootReducer from './reducers';

const store = createStore(rootReducer);
```
Here, `rootReducer` represents the combined reducers of your application. Reducers are functions that handle state updates based on dispatched actions.

### Step 3 — Wrap the application with a `<Provider>`
The `<Provider>` component from React Redux should wrap your application, providing the Redux store to all components that need access to the state.

```jsx
import { Provider } from 'react-redux';

ReactDOM.render(
  <Provider store={store}>
    <App />
  </Provider>,
  document.getElementById('root')
);
```

## 18.7 Redux middleware

### Redux Thunk
**Redux Thunk is a middleware that allows you to write action creators that return a function instead of an action.** This function can then be used to perform async logic and dispatch other actions.

### redux-saga
**redux-saga is a library that allows you to handle side effects in a Redux application by using generator functions.** It provides a way to handle async actions and to separate the logic for handling side effects from the rest of the application.

---

## 18.8 Redux vs Context API — when to use which

**React Context** is a built-in feature of React that allows you to share data between components without having to pass props down through multiple levels of the component tree.

**React Redux** is a library that allows you to connect your React components to a Redux store. It provides a way to access the state from the store and to dispatch actions to modify the state.

metadata.title: REACT-COMPLETE-NOTES
metadata.section: 18.8 Redux vs Context API — when to use which

text:
### Downsides of Redux compared to Flux
- The learning curve is steeper as it has a lot more concepts
- It can create **unnecessary complexity for small or simple applications**
- It can make debugging more difficult because the state is not visible in the components
- It can lead to verbose and repetitive code because actions and action creators are separate files

> **Practical guidance:** for a small app, start with `useState` and lift state up. Reach for Context when you have genuine cross-cutting global state (theme, auth). Reach for Redux only when the app is big enough that a predictable, centrally-logged state machine earns its complexity.

---

# PART 19 — Performance Optimization

## 19.1 The golden rule

> **Don't optimize prematurely.**
>
> Memoization and virtualization add complexity and can even **hurt** performance if used blindly. **Profile first**, fix real bottlenecks, and prefer structural fixes (state placement, composition) over reflexive `memo()`.
>
> **Measure before you memoize.**

---

## 19.2 The 12 key optimization techniques

### 01 — Image Optimization
Optimizing images can significantly reduce the load time of your application.

**Implementation:**
- Use modern image formats (e.g. **WebP**) and tools for compressing images.
- Serve **appropriately sized** images based on the user's device.

*(Recall: media — images — is what takes the longest to load on most websites.)*

---

## 19.3 Virtualization

**Implement virtualization techniques for large lists or tables to render only the visible portion of the content**, rather than rendering the entire list.

Libraries like **`react-virtualized`** and **`react-window`** can help with virtualizing large data sets.

> **Large unvirtualized lists are a top performance killer.** Use stable keys and virtualize for 1000+ rows.

---

## 19.4 Performance profiling

Use tools like the **React Profiler**, **React DevTools**, or **browser DevTools** to identify performance bottlenecks in the application. Measure and optimize components or operations that cause performance issues, such as **excessive re-renders or inefficient data fetching**.

```jsx
<Profiler id="App" onRender={logRender}>
  <App />
</Profiler>
```

**Measure before optimizing — don't guess.**

---

## 19.5 State placement

- **Keep state as local as possible;** lift only when shared.
- **Move fast-changing state into the smallest component that needs it.** This prevents parent trees from re-rendering unnecessarily.
- **Global state re-renders everything subscribed to it.**

---

## 19.6 The common performance mistakes (checklist)

- ❌ Wrapping every component in `memo()`
- ❌ Memoizing cheap calculations
- ❌ Creating new objects/arrays inline as props (in hot render paths)
- ❌ Storing derived data in state instead of computing it
- ❌ Skipping the Profiler and guessing
- ❌ Using arrow functions in render methods *(they create a new function on every render, which can negatively impact performance and cause children to re-render even when props haven't changed)*
- ❌ Large unvirtualized lists
- ❌ Using array indexes as keys in reorderable lists

---
---

# PART 20 — Testing

## 20.1 Why test?

Testing is an essential part of the software development process, and React provides several testing frameworks and libraries widely used in the React ecosystem.

**These frameworks help ensure that React components and features are working as expected and that any changes to the codebase do not introduce regressions.**

---

## 20.2 The two main tools

### Jest
**Jest is a popular JavaScript testing framework** widely used for testing utilities including **assertions, test runners, and mocking capabilities**. Jest is known for its **simplicity, speed and ease of use**. It supports both **unit testing and integration testing** of React components and provides seamless integration with React through the **`react-test-renderer`** package.

### React Testing Library
**React Testing Library is a testing utility that encourages testing components from the user's perspective.** It provides a simple and intuitive API for querying and interacting with React components in a way that closely mimics how users would interact with the actual application.

**React Testing Library promotes testing the behaviour and output of components rather than their implementation details**, resulting in more robust and maintainable tests.

---

# PART 21 — Best Practices, Debugging and Common Mistakes

## 21.1 Best practices for organising and structuring React code

### Component Organization
Organise components into **logical and reusable units**. Use a component-based architecture, where **each component has a single responsibility** and can be easily reused in different parts of the application.

metadata.title: REACT-COMPLETE-NOTES
metadata.section: PART 21 — Best Practices, Debugging and Common Mistakes

text:
### File Structure
Follow a **consistent file structure** to keep the codebase organized. Consider grouping related files together — such as components, styles and tests — to improve maintainability and ease of navigation.

> **Note:** React doesn't have opinions on how you put files into folders. Some developers group their files by **feature**. When moving files into folders, remember to **export** them so you can import them where necessary.

### Container and Presentational Components
Implement the **container-presentational component pattern**:
- **Container components** are responsible for managing state, handling data, fetching, and interacting with the Redux store.
- **Presentational components** focus on rendering UI elements and receiving props to display data.

### Separate concerns
Keep concerns separated between components. **Separate rendering logic from business logic**, and avoid mixing presentational code and state-management code in the same component.

### Use React hooks
Utilize React hooks such as `useState`, `useEffect` and `useContext` to manage component state, handle side effects and share state across components. **Hooks provide a more concise and readable way to write functional components.**

### Maintain Readability
Write clean, readable code by:
- Following **naming conventions**
- Using **descriptive variable and function names**
- **Commenting** when necessary
- **Breaking down complex components** into smaller, more manageable functions or components

### Config files
Create a **config file** (also called a **constants file**) in your project. Put all hardcoded values into it:

```js
// config.js
export const IMG_CDN_URL = "https://some-cdn-url/";
export const restaurantList = [ /* ... */ ];
```
Then import where needed:
```jsx
import { IMG_CDN_URL } from "./config";
```

---

## 21.2 Module exports and imports

There are **2 ways of exporting**:

### (i) Default export
- This is the **default** way.
- It means you want to export **only one** value.
- **There can be only one default export per module.**

```jsx
const Header = () => { /* ... */ };
export default Header;
```
```jsx
import Header from "./components/Header";
```
The imported name is given **locally** to the variable and **doesn't have to match** the original export name.

### (ii) Named exports ```jsx export const Title = () => { /* ... */ }; ``` ```jsx import { Title } from "./components/Header"; ``` Named exports **must** match the exported name (unless aliased). ### Both together | Header.js | App.js | |---|---| | `export const Title = () => {..}`
`const Header = () => {..}`
`export default Header` | `import Header, { Title } from "./components/Header";` |

### Importing everything
```jsx
import * as Obj from "./components/Header";
// then use Obj.Title, Obj.Header
```

> **When you are using a component in the same file, you don't have to export it at all.**

> A **module** is a self-contained unit that can expose assets to other modules using `export`, and acquire assets from other modules using `import`.

---

## 21.3 Debugging and troubleshooting common issues

### 1. Use developer tools
Leverage the browser's developer tools — such as the **JavaScript console** and **React DevTools** — to debug and inspect your React application. **These tools provide insights into component hierarchies, state changes, and potential errors.**

### 2. Debugging techniques
Implement **console logging** or use the **`debugger`** statement to examine variable values, track a component's lifecycle, or identify unexpected behaviour. This can help pinpoint the source of issues.

### 3. Error handling
Implement proper error handling techniques such as:
- **`try...catch` blocks**
- **Error boundaries**
- **Global error handling components** like `componentDidCatch`

This ensures that errors are **caught and gracefully handled**, preventing application crashes or unexpected behaviour.

### 4. Testing and linting
Write **unit tests** for React components and use **linting tools like ESLint** to catch common coding errors and enforce best practices. **Testing and linting can help identify issues early in the development process and improve code quality.**

---

## 21.4 Error boundaries

**Error boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI.**

They were introduced in **React v16** and they allow you to handle errors gracefully and ensure that your application continues to function even if there is an error.

### Error boundaries vs try/catch

| try/catch block | Error boundary |
|---|---|
| Works with **imperative** code | Meant for **declarative** code to render on the screen |
| A **language-level construct** that lets you handle exceptions occurring during the execution of the code inside the block | A **React component** that catches JS errors anywhere in its child component tree, logs them, and displays a fallback UI |
| Used to handle exceptions in JavaScript | Used specifically to handle errors in a React application |

```jsx
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<Oops />}>
  <Widget />
</ErrorBoundary>
```

---

## 21.5 Strict Mode

**Strict mode is a development-only feature in React that highlights potential problems in an application.** When a component is rendered in strict mode, React runs **extra checks and warnings** for any potential issues. This helps you identify and fix problems before they become bigger issues.

| Mistake | ❌ DON'T | ✅ DO |
|---|---|---|
| **Missing Keys** | `list.map(i => <Row {...i} />)` | `list.map(i => <Row key={i.id} {...i} />)` |
| **Bad Controlled/Uncontrolled** | `<input value={v} />` — no onChange | `<input value={v} onChange={onChange} />` |
| **Wrong useEffect Deps** | `useEffect(() => { load(id); }, [])` | `useEffect(() => { load(id); }, [id])` |
| **State Sync Problems** | `useEffect(() => setLocal(prop), [prop])` | Derive during render, or lift state up |
| **Unnecessary useEffect** | `useEffect(() => setFull(a+b), [a,b])` |

## 21.7 The Golden Rules

> **Derive, don't sync · keep state local · let Actions own async status · measure before you memoize · push data-fetching to the server when you can.**

### Best practices checklist
- Small components
- Compose over inherit
- Derive, don't sync
- Stable keys always
- Keep state local
- Push data-fetching to the server
- Profile first
- `memo()` sparingly

### Component pattern best practices

| Pattern | Best practice |
|---|---|
| **Functional Components** | Default in modern React — class components are legacy |
| **Props** | Treat props as read-only; never mutate them |
| **Children** | Enables flexible composition without prop explosion |
| **Conditional Rendering** | Avoid nested ternaries — extract to a variable or component |
| **Lists & Keys** | Never use array index as key if list can reorder |
| **Event Handling** | Avoid inline object/array literals in hot render paths |
| **Controlled Components** | React state is the single source of truth |
| **Uncontrolled Components** | Read via ref on submit; good for simple/perf-sensitive forms |
| **Composition** | Prefer composition over deep prop drilling or inheritance |
| **Custom Hooks** | Extract reusable stateful logic; prefix with `use` |

## 22.4 Config-Driven UI

**All of the UI (say, the Swiggy home page) is driven by a config which is sent by the backend (the API).**

### Why?
Swiggy should work in Kolkata, Dehradun, Delhi and whatever location — and we should show different website information for each location. To do that, we control our front-end using a **config**. This is why it is known as **Config Driven UI**. **All of it is controlled by the backend.**

### The bug you will hit — and why you need TWO state variables

**The bug:** after one search, the state gets updated. Then when you search again, it doesn't work.

**The cause:** `restaurants` gets filtered *down*. The next search then filters the already-filtered list.

**The fix:** you should never overwrite the master list. **Maintain 2 variables:**
- **Var 1** ⇒ the list of **all** restaurants
- **Var 2** ⇒ the list of **filtered** restaurants

```jsx
const [allRestaurants, setAllRestaurants] = useState([]);
const [filteredRestaurants, setFilteredRestaurants] = useState([]);
```

Whenever you filter, you **filter from `allRestaurants`**. You **display `filteredRestaurants`** in the UI. On the first API call, set both to the same data.

# PART 23 — React 19: The Modern APIs

*Once you have the fundamentals from Parts 1–22, this is what modern React adds.*

## 23.1 React 19 overview

React 19 refines the mental model introduced by **Concurrent Rendering**: **less imperative state-syncing, more declarative async.**

The headline additions — **Actions, `use()`, and native form integration** — remove the boilerplate that used to surround loading states, pending UI, and optimistic updates.

**Server Components** and **Server Functions** push data-fetching and mutations onto the server by default, shrinking client bundles without leaving the component model.

### What is React 19?
A major release focused on **simplifying async UI, forms, and the client/server boundary** while keeping the component model you already know.

### Key improvements
Fewer hooks needed for common async work, native form handling, faster hydration, and first-class metadata & resource loading.

### The full feature list

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Server Components** | Components that render on the server, ship **zero JS** to the client, and can read data directly — no client-side fetch waterfall. |
| **Actions** | Async functions passed to forms, transitions, or event handlers. **React manages pending, error, and optimistic state for you.** |
| **New Form APIs** | `<form action={fn}>` now accepts async functions directly — no manual `preventDefault`, fetch, or state wiring. |
| **`use()` API** | Reads the value of a Promise or Context **during render** — works conditionally, unlike other hooks. |
| **ref as a Prop** | Function components can accept `ref` directly as a prop — **`forwardRef` is no longer required**. |
| **Improved Hydration** | Better mismatch diagnostics and more resilient hydration that recovers gracefully from third-party DOM edits. |
| **Metadata Support** | `<title>`, `<meta>`, and `<link>` can be rendered **anywhere in the tree** — React hoists them into `<head>` automatically. |
| **Stylesheet Support** | `<link rel="stylesheet">` with precedence hints lets React control load order and dedupe styles across the tree. |
| **Preloading APIs** | `preload`, `preinit`, `prefetchDNS` and `preconnect` (from `react-dom`) give components fine-grained control over resource loading. |
| **Error Handling** | `onCaughtError` / `onUncaughtError` root options plus clearer error boundaries reduce noisy duplicate logging. |

---

## 23.2 The new React 19 APIs and hooks

### `use()`
Reads a **Promise or Context value during render**.
```jsx
const data = use(promise);
const theme = use(ThemeContext);
```
> **Can be called conditionally — unlike other hooks.** The Promise must stay stable across renders.

### `useActionState()`
Tracks **pending / result / error** state for an Action.
```jsx
const [state, formAction, pending] = useActionState(updateName, null);
```
> Use for any form or button that calls an async function. Returns `[state, dispatchAction, pending]`.

### `useOptimistic()`
Shows **instant optimistic UI** while an Action is in flight.
```jsx
const [opt, addOpt] = useOptimistic(
  list,
  (s, item) => [...s, item]
);
```
> **Automatically reverts if the underlying Action throws.**

## 23.4 Server and Client Components

### The comparison table

| Concept | Runs Where | Ships JS? | Can Use Hooks / State? | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Client-side Rendering** | Browser | Yes | Yes | Interactive widgets, forms |
| **Server Rendering (SSR)** | Server, then hydrates | Yes | Yes | Fast first paint + interactivity |
| **Server Components** | Server only | **No** | **No** (no `useState`/`useEffect`) | Data-heavy, static-ish UI |
| **Client Components** | Server (SSR) + Browser | Yes | Yes | Anything with interaction |

### Loading & error states
Wrap async Server Components in `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` for loading UI, and an **error boundary** (or a route-level `error.js` in frameworks) to catch rejected data fetches.

---

## 23.5 Server Side Rendering (SSR)

**To implement Server Side Rendering in a React application, you can use a library such as Next.js or `ReactDOMServer`.** These libraries allow you to render your React components on the **server** and send the resulting HTML to the browser.

This can improve the performance of your application by **reducing the initial load time** and providing a better experience for **search engines**.

### Next.js — major features
**NextJS is a framework for building web applications with React.** It provides a set of features for building server-rendered React applications:
- **Server-side rendering (SSR)** out of the box
- **Automatic code splitting** for faster load times
- Built-in **development server with hot reloading**
- Easy setup for custom routes with **file-system based routing**
- **Static site generation (SSG)**

---

## 23.6 The React 19 Decision Guide

**"Which hook or API do I need?"** — Start with the question closest to your problem. **Most rendering bugs trace back to picking the wrong tool here — especially reaching for `useEffect` when a derived value or an Action would do.**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Need local state? | → `useState` / `useReducer` |
| Need a side effect after render? | → `useEffect` |
| Need a mutable value with no re-render? | → `useRef` |
| Need state shared across components? | → Context, or an external store |
| Need to read an async resource? | → `use()` |
| Need form pending/result state? | → `useActionState()` |
| Need instant optimistic UI? | → `useOptimistic()` |
| Need a form's pending status in a child? | → `useFormStatus()` |
| Need to reduce bundle size? | → Server Components / `lazy()` |
| Need a performance optimization? | → **Profile first** → memoize only if proven |

# SECTION A — React basics, the DOM and JSX

## 1. What are the advantages and disadvantages of React?

**Advantages** of React include its ability to handle complex user interfaces, its flexibility and reusability of components, and its performance optimization through the use of a virtual DOM.

**Disadvantages** include a steep learning curve for beginners and the need for additional libraries or tools to complete a full-featured application.

text:
## 2. What does DOM stand for?

DOM stands for **Document Object Model**.

---

## 3. What is Virtual DOM?

Virtual DOM is a **lightweight in-memory representation of the actual DOM**. It is used to improve the performance of updates and changes to the actual DOM by **reducing the number of expensive DOM manipulations**.

---

## 4. How does Virtual DOM work?

Virtual DOM works by **comparing the current virtual DOM tree with a new virtual DOM tree**, and then applying the **minimal set of changes** to the actual DOM. This allows React to efficiently update the user interface without causing unnecessary re-renders or layout changes.

```
Virtual DOM:   State Change  →  Compute Diff  →  Re-render
Browser DOM:   only the nodes that actually changed get updated
```

---

## 5. What is the difference between Shadow DOM and Virtual DOM?

**Shadow DOM** refers to a feature of **web browsers** that allows developers to create a separate DOM tree, called a shadow tree, that is attached to a specific element and is hidden from the main document.

**Virtual DOM** is a concept used **in React** to optimize the performance of updates to the user interface, whereas **Shadow DOM** is a feature of web browsers that allows for **scoping of CSS and JavaScript** within a specific element.

---

## 6. What are the differences between Real DOM and Virtual DOM?

**Real DOM** is the actual tree-like structure of a web page, which can be manipulated directly to change the layout or content of the page.

**Virtual DOM** is a lightweight in-memory representation of the actual DOM, which is used to optimize the performance of updates to the user interface.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 6. What are the differences between Real DOM and Virtual DOM?

text:
## 7. What is React Fiber?

React Fiber is a **new reconciliation algorithm that was introduced in React 16**. It is designed to improve the performance and flexibility of React by **breaking down the render process into smaller, asynchronous chunks**.

---

## 8. What is the main goal of React Fiber?

The main goal of React Fiber is to **improve the performance and responsiveness** of web applications by breaking down the render process into smaller, asynchronous chunks. This allows React to more effectively utilize the **main thread** and to better handle complex user interfaces.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 8. What is the main goal of React Fiber?

text:
## 9. What is reconciliation?

Reconciliation is the process that React uses to determine the **minimal set of changes** to be made to the actual DOM. It compares the current virtual DOM tree with a new virtual DOM tree, and then applies the minimal set of changes to the actual DOM.

```
Virtual DOM  --Diff-->  New Virtual DOM  --Update-->  Browser DOM
```

---

## 10. What is JSX?

JSX is a **syntax extension for JavaScript** that allows developers to write **HTML-like elements** in their JavaScript code. It is commonly used in React to describe the structure and content of a component's user interface.

---

## 11. Can browsers read a JSX file?

**No.** Browsers cannot read JSX files directly. They must be **transpiled** — converted — to JavaScript before they can be interpreted by the browser. (Babel does this.)

---

## 12. Explain how Virtual DOM works.

Virtual DOM is a lightweight, in-memory representation of the actual DOM. It is used to improve the performance of updates and changes to the actual DOM by reducing the number of expensive DOM manipulations.

When a component's **state or props change**, React will create a **new virtual DOM tree**, compare it to the previous tree, and then apply **only the minimal set of changes** necessary to the actual DOM. This improves the performance of the application and reduces the number of unnecessary re-renders.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 11. Can browsers read a JSX file?

text:
## 13. What are React components?

**In React, everything is a component.** A component is a **small, reusable piece of code** that represents a part of a user interface.

Components can be defined as either a **class** or a **function** and can include a combination of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. These components can also be **nested and reused** throughout the application, which makes it easy to manage and maintain the application's user interface.

---

## 14. What is the meaning of the component-based architecture of React?

The component-based architecture of React allows developers to build complex user interfaces by **breaking them down into smaller, reusable components**. Each component can manage its own state and props, and can be easily reused throughout the application. This structure makes it easy to **understand, test, and maintain** the application's codebase.

---
---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 14. What is the meaning of the component-based architecture of React?

# SECTION B — Component types, state and props

## 15. What are functional components?

Functional components in React are simply **JavaScript functions that return a React element**. They do not (traditionally) have state or lifecycle methods and are used for simple, stateless components.

> *Note: since React 16.8, hooks give functional components state and lifecycle behaviour.*

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION B — Component types, state and props

text:
## 16. What are class components in React?

Class components in React are defined using the **ES6 class syntax**. They have access to **state and lifecycle methods** and are used for more complex, stateful components.

---

## 17. What is the difference between functional and class components in React?

The main difference is that **functional components are simpler** and do not (natively) have state or lifecycle methods, whereas **class components have access to state and lifecycle methods** and are more powerful.

Additionally, **functional components use hooks for state management**.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 16. What are class components in React?

text:
## 18. How to use CSS in React?

In React, CSS can be added to a component in several ways:
- Using **inline styles**
- Using a **CSS file** and importing it into the component
- Using a **CSS preprocessor** like Sass or Less
- Using a **CSS-in-JS library** like styled-components

*(Also: CSS Modules — see the notes.)*

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 18. How to use CSS in React?

text:
## 19. How does rendering work in React?

React's rendering process begins when a component's **state or props change**. React creates a new virtual DOM tree, compares it to the previous tree, and then applies only the minimal set of changes necessary to the actual DOM. **This process is called reconciliation.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 19. How does rendering work in React?

text:
## 20. What are states in React?

State in React is an **object that holds data that can change**, and it is managed by a component. It is used to store and update the component's data and can be passed down to child components as props.

State can be updated using the **`setState`** method, which triggers a **re-render** of the component, updating the user interface.

---

## 21. What are props in React?

Props in React are used to **pass data from a parent component to a child component**. They are essentially a way to pass data and methods down the component tree. **Props are read-only**, meaning that they cannot be modified by the child component.

---

## 22. What is the `children` prop?

The children prop is a **special prop** used to pass child elements to a component. It is used to pass elements between components, such as a list of items or a set of nested components.

---

## 23. What is a higher-order component in React?

A **higher-order component (HOC)** is a **function that takes a component as an argument and returns a new component with additional functionality**. HOCs are used to **reuse component logic**, such as authentication or performance optimization.

```jsx
const NewComponent = higherOrderComponent(WrappedComponent);
```

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 23. What is a higher-order component in React?

text:
## 24. How to create a props proxy for an HOC component?

To create a props proxy for an HOC component, you can use the **`React.forwardRef`** function. This function allows you to **pass props through to the wrapped component**, preserving the original component's props.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 24. How to create a props proxy for an HOC component?

text:
## 25. What are controlled components?

Controlled components are components that are **controlled by the state of the parent component**. The parent component manages the component's state, and the child component's behavior is determined by the parent component's state.

---

## 26. What are uncontrolled components?

Uncontrolled components are components that **manage their own state internally**, and their behavior is not determined by the parent component's state.

---

## 27. How to update state in React class components?

To update state in a React class component, use the **`setState`** method. This method takes an **object or a function** as an argument, and it will **merge** the new state with the existing state.

---

## 28. How to update state in a React functional component?

To update state in a React functional component, use the **`useState`** hook. This hook returns an **array** containing the current state and a function to update it.

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 28. How to update state in a React functional component?

text:
## 29. How to differentiate between state and props?

**State** is the **internal** data of a component that can change and is managed by the component itself.
**Props** are **external** data passed to a component from its parent component.

**State can be updated by the component, whereas props cannot be updated by the component.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 29. How to differentiate between state and props?

text:
## 30. What is "Lifting State Up" in React?

Lifting state up refers to the process of **moving state management from a child component to its parent component**. This is done to make the state more easily accessible and manageable for the entire component tree.

---
---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 30. What is "Lifting State Up" in React?

text:
# SECTION C — Events

## 31. What is an Event in React?

An event in React is a way to **respond to user interactions** such as clicks, hover, or form submissions.

---

## 32. How to handle events in React (for both functional and class components)?

In React, events are handled using the **`on`** keyword, followed by the event name and a callback function. For example, to handle a button click event, use `onClick={handleClick}`. This works in both functional and class components.

---

## 33. What is the difference between HTML and React event handling?

In **HTML**, events are handled using event attributes such as `onclick` or `onchange` (lowercase, string values).

In **React**, events are handled using the **`on` keyword** (camelCase) and a **callback function**. React's event handling system is more powerful and flexible than the traditional HTML event handling system.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 33. What is the difference between HTML and React event handling?

text:
## 34. What are synthetic events in React?

Synthetic events in React are a **cross-browser compatible way to handle events**. They are used to **normalize the behavior of different browser event systems** and provide a **consistent API** for handling events.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 34. What are synthetic events in React?

text:
## 35. How to pass a parameter to an event handler?

To pass a parameter to an event handler, use an **arrow function** to wrap the event handler:

```jsx
<button onClick={() => handleClick(parameter)}>
```

---
---

## 36. What are React Hooks?

React Hooks are **functions that allow you to use state and other React features in functional components**. They were introduced in **React 16.8**.

---

## 37. When were React Hooks first introduced?

React Hooks were first introduced in **React 16.8, in 2019**.

---

## 44. Can you create your own custom React hooks?

**Yes.** You can create custom React hooks by following the naming convention **"use"** and using state and other hooks inside them.

---

## 45. What do you need to keep in mind while creating custom React hooks?

- They should **only call other hooks at the top level** and not inside loops or conditions.
- Make sure the hook **only performs one specific action**.

---

# SECTION E — Context, Router, Pure Components and keys

## 46. What is the Context API in React?

The Context API allows you to **share data between components without passing props through every level of the component tree**. It provides a way for components to access data that is **"global" to the component tree**, such as a user's authentication status or a theme.

The Context API consists of a **Provider** component, which provides the data, and a **Consumer** component, which accesses the data.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION E — Context, Router, Pure Components and keys

text:
## 47. What is React Router?

React Router is a **library for routing in React apps**. It allows you to define the different routes in your application and render the appropriate components for each route. This makes it easy to **change the displayed content based on the current URL, without having to refresh the page**.

---

## 48. What are Pure components and what is their purpose?

Pure components are components that **only re-render if their props or state have changed**. They are optimized for performance, and they can improve the performance of your application by **reducing the number of unnecessary re-renders**.

Pure components are also known as "functional components" or "stateless components" and they are defined by a function.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 48. What are Pure components and what is their purpose?

text:
## 49. Can you update React state directly?

**No.** You cannot update React state directly. You should always use the **`setState`** method (or the `useState` setter) to update the state, which will trigger a re-render of the component.

---

## 50. What is the purpose of the callback function as an argument of `setState()`?

The callback function passed as an argument to `setState` is called **after the state has been updated and the component has re-rendered**. It can be used to perform any **additional actions**, such as sending a network request, that depend on the updated state.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 49. Can you update React state directly?

text:
## 51. What is the "key" prop and what is the benefit of using it in arrays of elements?

The **"key" prop** is used to give a **unique identifier** to each item in an array of elements. When elements are re-rendered, React uses the key to identify **which elements have changed, been added, or been removed**. This allows React to **update the DOM efficiently**, improving the performance of the application.

---
---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 51. What is the "key" prop and what is the benefit of using it in arrays of elements?

# SECTION F — Lifecycle, setState and strict mode

## 52. What are the different phases of the component lifecycle in React?

1. **Mounting** — When a component is being added to the DOM.
2. **Updating** — When a component's props or state change.
3. **Unmounting** — When a component is being removed from the DOM.

*(TopperWorld notes also list an **Initial Phase** before mounting, containing `getDefaultProps()` and `getInitialState()`.)*

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION F — Lifecycle, setState and strict mode

text:
## 53. What are the lifecycle methods of React?

The lifecycle methods are methods called at specific points during the lifecycle of a component:

- **`constructor`** — Called before the component is added to the DOM.
- **`render`** — Called whenever the component needs to update the DOM.
- **`componentDidMount`** — Called **after** the component has been added to the DOM.
- **`componentDidUpdate`** — Called **after** the component has been updated.
- **`componentWillUnmount`** — Called **before** the component is removed from the DOM.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 53. What are the lifecycle methods of React?

text:
## 54. What is the purpose of using the super constructor with the props argument?

The purpose of using **`super(props)`** is to **call the constructor of the parent class and pass in the props**. It is necessary because the parent class's constructor sets up the initial state and props of the component and **must be called before the child class's constructor** can use `this`.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 54. What is the purpose of using the super constructor with the props argument?

text:
## 55. Why does React use `className` over the `class` attribute?

React uses the `className` attribute instead of the `class` attribute because **`class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript**. Using `className` avoids any confusion and ensures that the attribute will be interpreted as intended.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 55. Why does React use `className` over the `class` attribute?

text:
## 56. What are fragments?

A **fragment** is a way to **group a list of children without adding extra nodes to the DOM**. It allows you to return multiple elements from a component's render method without wrapping them in an additional DOM node.

Fragments are represented by an empty JSX tag: **`<>`** and **`</>`** (or `<React.Fragment>`).

---

## 57. Why are fragments better than container divs?

Fragments are better because they **don't add an extra node to the DOM**. This makes the rendered HTML **cleaner and more efficient**, especially when a component renders a list of items. Additionally, **it helps with accessibility** because it doesn't create an unnecessary wrapper element around the content.

*(The TopperWorld notes add: fragments make execution of code faster compared to a div tag, and take less memory.)*

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 57. Why are fragments better than container divs?

text:
## 58. What are stateless components?

Stateless components — also known as **functional components** — are components that **don't have any internal state**. They are defined as a function, they receive props and they return JSX to be rendered.

They are **simpler, easier to reason about and less prone to bugs** than stateful components because they don't have lifecycle methods.

---

## 59. What are error boundaries in React v16?

**Error boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI.**

They were introduced in **React v16**, and they allow you to handle errors gracefully and ensure that your application continues to function even if there is an error.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 59. What are error boundaries in React v16?

text:
## 60. What is the use of the `react-dom` package?

The `react-dom` package **provides the renderer for React components**. It provides the functions that are used to **render React components on the web (DOM)**.

---

## 61. What will happen if you use `setState()` in the constructor?

If you use `setState` in the constructor, it will cause the component to **re-render before it is added to the DOM**. This can cause **unexpected behavior and should be avoided**.

Instead, it is recommended to **initialize the state with the constructor's props** and use `setState` in **`componentDidMount`**.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 60. What is the use of the `react-dom` package?

text:
## 62. What is the impact of using indexes as keys?

Using indexes as keys can have a **negative impact on performance** because they **don't provide a stable identity** for elements, and React has to rely on the **order of elements** in the array to determine which elements have changed. **This can lead to unnecessary re-renders.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 62. What is the impact of using indexes as keys?

text:
## 63. How do you implement Server Side Rendering (SSR)?

To implement SSR in a React application, you can use a library such as **Next.js** or **ReactDOMServer**. These libraries allow you to **render your React components on the server** and send the resulting HTML to the browser.

This can improve the performance of your application by **reducing the initial load time** and providing a **better experience for search engines**.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 63. How do you implement Server Side Rendering (SSR)?

text:
## 64. What is the lifecycle methods order in mounting?

1. `constructor()`
2. `static getDerivedStateFromProps()`
3. `render()`
4. `componentDidMount()`

---

## 65. Which lifecycle methods are going to be deprecated in React v16?

- `componentWillMount`
- `componentWillReceiveProps`
- `componentWillUpdate`

---

metadata.section: 64. What is the lifecycle methods order in mounting?

## 66. What is the purpose of the `getDerivedStateFromProps()` lifecycle method?

Its purpose is to provide a way to **synchronize a component's internal state with its props**. This lifecycle method is called **before `render()`** and it allows you to update the internal state based on changes in the props.

**It is used as an alternative to `componentWillReceiveProps()`.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 66. What is the purpose of the `getDerivedStateFromProps()` lifecycle method?

text:
## 67. What is the purpose of the `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate()` lifecycle method?

Its purpose is to **capture some information from the DOM before it is potentially changed**. This lifecycle method is called **right before the browser updates the DOM** and it allows you to capture the **current scroll position** or other information that you might want to use later.

---

metadata.section: 67. What is the purpose of the `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate()` lifecycle method?

metadata.section: 68. Why do we need to pass a function to `setState()`?

## 69. What is strict mode in React?

**Strict mode is a development-only feature** in React that **highlights potential problems** in an application. When a component is rendered in strict mode, React will run **extra checks and warnings** for any potential issues. This can help you identify and fix problems before they become a bigger issue.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 69. What is strict mode in React?

## 70. Can a component re-render without calling `setState`?

**Yes.** You can force a component to re-render without calling `setState` by **changing its `key` prop**. This will cause React to **treat the component as a new one** and it will re-render it.

This can be useful in some cases, but **it's generally not recommended** because it can cause unnecessary re-renders and negatively impact performance.

---

metadata.section: 70. Can a component re-render without calling `setState`?

# SECTION G — React vs ReactDOM, bundling and code splitting

## 71. What is the difference between React and ReactDOM?

**React** is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. It provides a way to build reusable UI components and manage their state.

**ReactDOM** is a **separate library** that provides specific methods for interacting with the DOM, such as **`render()`** and **`unmountComponentAtNode()`**.

**ReactDOM is the glue that connects React with the DOM.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION G — React vs ReactDOM, bundling and code splitting

text:
## 72. Why is ReactDOM separated from React?

React and ReactDOM are separated to allow for **better flexibility in different environments**. React can be used to build user interfaces on the **web, on mobile, or on desktop** without having to change the core library. ReactDOM provides the specific methods needed to render components **on the web**.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 72. Why is ReactDOM separated from React?

text:
## 73. Is it possible to use React without rendering HTML?

**Yes.** React can be used to build user interfaces for other environments such as **native mobile apps or virtual reality**. **React Native** and **React VR** are examples of libraries that allow you to use React to build apps for those environments.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 73. Is it possible to use React without rendering HTML?

text:
## 74. You can't update props in React. Why?

You can't update props because they are **passed down from a parent component and are considered immutable**. Instead, you should **use state** to manage data that can change within a component, and pass that data down to child components as props.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 74. You can't update props in React. Why?

text:
## 75. How to focus an input element on page load?

Use the **`ref`** property to create a reference to the input element, and then call the **`focus()`** method on that reference in the **`componentDidMount()`** lifecycle method.

*(In a functional component: call `inputRef.current.focus()` inside a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array.)*

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 75. How to focus an input element on page load?

text:
## 76. How to programmatically trigger a click event in React?

Use the **`ref`** property to create a reference to the element, and then call the **`click()`** method on that reference.

---

## 77. What is bundling in React and why do we use it?

**Bundling is the process of combining multiple JavaScript files into a single file.** This is done to **reduce the number of network requests** needed to load an application and to **improve the performance** of the application.

There are various bundlers such as **webpack, rollup, parcel, and browserify**.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 76. How to programmatically trigger a click event in React?

text:
## 78. What is code-splitting in React and why do we use it?

**Code-splitting is a technique that allows you to split your application's JavaScript code into smaller chunks.** This can improve performance by **only loading the code that is needed for the current page or component**. This technique is usually used in combination with a bundler like webpack.

---
---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 78. What is code-splitting in React and why do we use it?

# SECTION H — Flux, Redux and React Native

## 79. What is Flux?

**Flux is an architecture for managing the state of an application.** It is designed to be used with React and it provides a **unidirectional data flow**, where data is passed down through components in a hierarchical structure.

```
Action ──▶ Dispatcher ──▶ Stores ──▶ Views ──▶ Action  (loop)
```

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: SECTION H — Flux, Redux and React Native

text:
## 80. What is Redux? Do you know any alternatives?

**Redux is a library for managing the state of an application.** It provides a **centralized store** to hold the state, and it uses **actions and reducers** to manage state changes.

**Alternatives to Redux:** Mobx, Apollo, and Unstated-next.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 80. What is Redux? Do you know any alternatives?

text:
## 81. What are the core principles of Redux?

1. **The state of the application is stored in a single immutable state tree.**
2. **The state can only be modified by emitting an action** — an object describing the change.
3. **To specify how the state tree is transformed by actions, you write pure reducers.**

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 81. What are the core principles of Redux?

text:
## 82. What are the downsides of Redux compared to Flux?

- **The learning curve is steeper** as it has a lot more concepts.
- It can create **unnecessary complexity for small or simple applications**.
- It can make **debugging more difficult** because the state is not visible in the components.
- It can lead to **verbose and repetitive code** because actions and action creators are separate files.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 82. What are the downsides of Redux compared to Flux?

text:
## 83. What is the difference between React Context and React Redux?

**React Context** is a **built-in feature of React** that allows you to share data between components without having to pass props down through multiple levels of the component tree.

**React Redux** is a **library** that allows you to connect your React components to a **Redux store**. It provides a way to access the state from the store and to dispatch actions to modify the state.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 83. What is the difference between React Context and React Redux?

text:
## 84. Why are Redux state functions called reducers?

Redux state functions are called reducers because they are used to **reduce** the current state and an action **to the next state**. The reducer takes the current state and an action as input and returns the next state.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 84. Why are Redux state functions called reducers?

text:
## 85. What is redux-saga?

**redux-saga is a library that allows you to handle side effects in a Redux application by using generator functions.** It provides a way to handle async actions and to **separate the logic for handling side effects** from the rest of the application.

---

## 86. What is Redux Thunk?

**Redux Thunk is a middleware that allows you to write action creators that return a function instead of an action.** This function can then be used to **perform async logic and dispatch other actions**.

---

## 87. What is the difference between React Native and React?

**React Native** is a **framework for building mobile applications** using React. It provides a way to use React to build apps for **iOS and Android**.

**React** is a **JavaScript library for building user interfaces**.

React Native uses a **subset of React** and provides **platform-specific components and APIs** to access the device's native features.

---
---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 87. What is the difference between React Native and React?

text:
# SECTION I — Advanced topics

## 88. What is render hijacking in React?

**Render hijacking is a technique that allows you to modify the rendered output of a component by wrapping it in another component.** The wrapping component can then **add or remove elements, change the styles, or modify the behavior** of the original component.

---

metadata.title: REACT-INTERVIEW-QUESTIONS
metadata.section: 89. What is the React memo function?

text:
## 90. What is the difference between a try-catch block and error boundaries?

**Try-catch blocks work with imperative code, whereas error boundaries are meant for declarative code to render on the screen.**

A **try-catch block** is a **language-level construct** that allows you to handle exceptions that occur during the execution of the code inside the block.

**Error boundaries** are **React components** that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI.

**Error boundaries are used specifically to handle errors in a React application, whereas try-catch blocks are used to handle exceptions in JavaScript.**

## 91. What is Next.js and what are its major features?

**Next.js is a framework for building web applications with React.** It provides a set of features for building server-rendered React applications, including:

- **Server-side rendering (SSR)** out of the box
- **Automatic code splitting** for faster load times
- **Built-in development server** with hot reloading
- **Easy setup for custom routes** with file-system based routing
- **Static site generation (SSG)**

---

## 92. Is it good to use arrow functions in render methods?

**It's generally not good.** Arrow functions in the render method **create a new function on every render**, which can **negatively impact performance**. If a component uses an arrow function in its render method, it will re-create that function on every render and **cause the component to re-render even if its props haven't changed**.

## 93. What is route-based code splitting?

**Route-based code splitting is a technique that allows you to split your application's JavaScript code into smaller chunks based on the routes in your application.** This can improve performance by **only loading the code that is needed for the current page or component**.

---

## 94. Is it possible to use React without JSX?

**Yes.** React provides a way to use JavaScript to create elements (`React.createElement`), and you can use JavaScript to create the same elements that you would create with JSX.

---

## 95. How to fetch data with React Hooks?

You can use the **`useEffect`** hook to fetch data in a React functional component. The `useEffect` hook allows you to run a side effect, such as fetching data, **after the component has rendered**. You can also use **`useState`** to store the fetched data and update the component when the data is available.

---

text:
## 96. What is Concurrent Rendering?

**Concurrent rendering is a feature of React that allows the browser to continue rendering the rest of the application while a component is being updated.** This can improve the user experience by providing **smoother animations** and **reducing the perceived time to load** the application.

---

## 97. What is the difference between async mode and concurrent mode?

**Async mode** is an **experimental feature** that allows React to **schedule updates and render components asynchronously**. This can improve the performance of an application by reducing the number of updates that need to be processed at the same time.

**Concurrent mode** is a feature that allows React to work in an asynchronous way.

---

- **Improved developer experience** with autocompletion and better error messages

## 100. What is the purpose of the `eslint` plugin for hooks?

The **ESLint plugin for hooks** is a set of rules that **enforces the rules of hooks as specified by the React team**. It helps to **prevent common mistakes and inconsistencies** when using hooks. It also helps to make sure that hooks are **only used in functional components** and that they are **called in the correct order**.

# SECTION J — React 19 interview questions

*Fourteen questions that come up in almost every modern React interview.*

## R1. What is new in React 19?

**Actions**, **`use()`**, **`useActionState`/`useOptimistic`/`useFormStatus`**, **ref as a prop**, **native form actions**, and **metadata/stylesheet/preload support**.

---

## R4. What is `useActionState()`?

A hook that **wires an Action to a piece of state**, returning **`[state, dispatchAction, pending]`**.

```jsx
const [state, formAction, pending] = useActionState(updateName, null);
```

---

## R5. What is `useOptimistic()`?

A hook that **renders an optimistic value immediately**, then **reconciles or reverts** once the real Action resolves.

```jsx
const [opt, addOpt] = useOptimistic(list, (s, item) => [...s, item]);
```

---

## R8. Server vs Client Components?

**Server Components can't use state/effects/browser APIs.**
**Client Components (`"use client"`) can — but they ship JS to the browser.**

---

## R9. What changed with refs?

**Function components can accept `ref` as a normal prop**, removing the need for **`forwardRef`** in most cases.

```jsx
function Input({ ref, ...props }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
}
```

---

## R10. When should you use `useMemo`?

**Only for genuinely expensive computations that measurably affect render time** — not for trivial arithmetic.

---

## R11. When should you use `useCallback`?

When a **function identity is passed to a memoized child** or used as an **effect dependency**.

---

## R12. `useEffect` vs event handlers?

**Effects sync with external systems after render.**
**User-triggered logic (clicks, submits) belongs in event handlers, not effects.**

---

## R13. Controlled vs uncontrolled?

**Controlled:** React state drives the input value.
**Uncontrolled:** the DOM holds the value, read via ref when needed.

---

## R14. How does reconciliation work?

**React diffs the new element tree against the previous one by type and key, updating only the DOM nodes that actually changed.**

---
---

text:
## The one-paragraph version

Every valid JavaScript file is a valid TypeScript file. You add annotations; `tsc` checks them and
then **deletes them**, emitting plain JavaScript. Nothing about runtime behaviour changes — no new
data structures, no new operators that survive compilation, no runtime type checking. If you're
debugging behaviour, you're debugging JavaScript. If you're fighting a red squiggle, you're fighting
a compiler that never sees your program run.

That single fact explains most of TypeScript's strangeness, and it's the thing to say out loud in an
interview.

```typescript
// what you write
function greet(name: string): string { return `Hi, ${name}`; }

// what actually runs
function greet(name) { return `Hi, ${name}`; }
```

## What's genuinely new — the whole list

| | JavaScript | TypeScript adds |
|---|---|---|
| Variables | `let x = 5` | `let x: number = 5` — and usually you omit it, because inference |
| Functions | `function f(a, b) {}` | Parameter and return types; optional and default params are typed |
| Objects | `{ name: "M" }` | `interface`/`type` describing the shape |
| Arrays | `[1, 2]` | `number[]`, and **tuples** — `[string, number]` |
| Reuse | Duck typing at runtime | **Generics** — type parameters checked at compile time |
| Null safety | Runtime `?.` and `??` | `strictNullChecks` — the compiler forces you to handle it |
| Narrowing | `typeof` checks you remember to write | The compiler *tracks* those checks and narrows the type |
| Enums | Object literals by convention | `enum` (a real runtime construct — the one exception to erasure) |
| Modules | ESM (JS §68) | Same, plus `import type` and `.d.ts` declaration files |
| Classes | ES6 classes (JS §41) | `public`/`private`/`protected`, `readonly`, `abstract`, parameter properties |

Everything else — closures, `this`, prototypes, async, the event loop — is **identical**. Your
JavaScript knowledge transfers whole.

## 1. Setup, `tsc`, and How It Fits a Project

```bash
npm i -D typescript @types/node
npx tsc --init            # creates tsconfig.json
npx tsc                   # compile
npx tsc --watch           # recompile on save
npx tsc --noEmit          # type-check only — what CI runs
```

**Three ways TypeScript reaches production:**

1. **`tsc` emits JavaScript** — the plain path. Slowest, but it type-checks.
2. **A bundler strips types** (esbuild, swc, Vite, Next.js) — fast, but **does not type-check**.
   You run `tsc --noEmit` separately in CI.
3. **Runtime strips types** (`ts-node`, Node 22+ with `--experimental-strip-types`, Bun, Deno).

Point 2 catches people out: your build passing does **not** mean your types are correct. Type
checking and bundling are separate jobs in most modern setups.

text:
### `let` vs `const` widening

```typescript
let a = "hello";       // string      — can be reassigned, so widened
const b = "hello";     // "hello"     — literal type
```

This matters constantly with unions:

```typescript
type Method = "GET" | "POST";
let m = "GET";                    // inferred string — NOT assignable to Method
const m2 = "GET";                 // inferred "GET"  — assignable
fetch(url, { method: m });        // ❌ error
fetch(url, { method: m2 });       // ✅
// fix for let: let m: Method = "GET";  or  as const
```

### Narrowing — the compiler follows your checks

```typescript
function format(value: string | number): string {
  if (typeof value === "string") {
    return value.toUpperCase();       // narrowed to string
  }
  return value.toFixed(2);            // narrowed to number — no else needed
}
```

Every narrowing mechanism:

```typescript
typeof x === "string"                 // primitives
x instanceof Date                     // classes
"role" in obj                         // property presence
Array.isArray(x)                      // arrays
if (x) { }                            // truthiness — removes null | undefined | "" | 0
x === null                            // equality
if (!user) return;                    // early return narrows the rest of the function
```

text:
### Custom type guards

```typescript
function isUser(x: unknown): x is User {          // "x is User" — a type predicate
  return typeof x === "object" && x !== null && "id" in x && "name" in x;
}

if (isUser(data)) { data.name; }                  // narrowed
```

`x is User` is a promise you make to the compiler — it doesn't verify your logic. A wrong type guard
is as dangerous as `any`. For real validation at a boundary, use **Zod** and get the type for free:

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";
const UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.number(), name: z.string() });
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;           // type derived from the validator
const user = UserSchema.parse(json);              // throws on bad data, and is typed
```

### `this` typing

```typescript
function handler(this: HTMLButtonElement, e: MouseEvent) {
  this.disabled = true;                    // `this` is typed, and erased at compile time
}
```

The rules for what `this` *is* are unchanged from JavaScript (**JS §37**). TypeScript only lets you
declare what you expect.

## 8. Generics

A type parameter — the same idea as Java generics, and one of the few places TypeScript is genuinely
new rather than annotation.

```typescript
function identity<T>(value: T): T { return value; }
identity("hi");            // T inferred as string
identity<number>(42);      // explicit

function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; }
```

Without generics you'd write `any` and lose the return type. With them, the relationship between
input and output is preserved.

### Generics vs `any`: same `T` in and out

`T` can be any type — `boolean`, `string`, `number`, an array, an object — but it is decided **once per
call**, and every place that uses `T` in that call must match. That is the difference from `any`.

```typescript
function idAny(value: any): any { return value; }
function idT<T>(value: T): T { return value; }

const a = idAny("hi");
a.toFixed(2);              // compiles, crashes at runtime: strings have no toFixed
const t = idT("hi");       // T = string, so t is a string
t.toFixed(2);              // ❌ caught while you write it
t.toUpperCase();           // ✅

idT(true);                 // T = boolean
idT(42);                   // T = number
idT([1, 2]);               // T = number[]
```

The parameter `value: T` and the return type `: T` are the same `T`, so the body can only return
something it knows is a `T`:

```typescript
function bad<T>(value: T): T {
  return "hello";          // ❌ T might be a number
}
```

Different letters mean different types: `function pair<T, U>(a: T, b: U): [T, U]`. In `first<T>(arr: T[])`
the `T` is the item type, so `first([1, 2, 3])` is `number | undefined` and `first(["a"])` is
`string | undefined`.
